data.body:
## Goal
- Two keyboard defects in the canvas context menu, both pre-existing and both
  verified in the pre-refactor binary, so neither was introduced by menu.js.
  The tab strip inherits both the moment it registers its own menu.

## Context
- Found while A/B-verifying `menu.js` against `git archive HEAD` in Chrome.
- Defect 1: arrow keys destroy the block menu. `menu.js`'s keydown calls
  `preventDefault()` but not `stopPropagation()`, so `app.js`'s nudge handler
  also fires. With a block selected, ArrowDown nudges it, which saves positions,
  which swaps, which fires `htmx:beforeSwap`, which closes the menu. Arrow
  navigation therefore only works on the empty-sheet menu, which clears the
  selection first.
- Defect 2: Escape's focus restore is a no-op. `#flow-canvas` has no `tabindex`,
  so `canvas().focus()` never lands and focus falls to `<body>`.

## Acceptance Criteria
- With a block selected and its context menu open, ArrowDown and ArrowUp move
  menu focus and do not nudge the block.
- Escape returns focus to the region the menu was raised from, for the canvas
  and for any other registered region.
- Both are covered by the CDP harness rather than asserted by eye.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./internal/web/...`
- Re-run the menu harness kept from the extraction task and show the two lines
  that previously read `menu present => false` and `tabindex => null`.

  is not supposed to do.

  throwaway build of the branch HEAD: `body.scrollWidth 983 > 860` there too, so
  it arrived with the tab strip rather than with the editing layer.

  rules and their responsive overrides.

  no coarser than 20px rather than at four fixed widths.

  presentation changes.

## Goal
- Kill the two ~60-line name switches `setParameter` and `parameterText` in internal/studio/catalog.go by making each parameter field definition own how its value is read from and written to `Parameters`.

## Context
- `parameterDefinition` (catalog.go:34) already carries name/label/type/step/min/max/unit/help. Add per-field behavior: `set(*Parameters, string) error` and `text(Parameters) string`. The `numberField` helper can build both from a `*Parameters -> *float64` field selector, so scalar fields stay one line each.
- Decision (recorded in the container): keep the flat `Parameters` union struct in model.go and the existing JSON wire format unchanged. Per-kind parameter structs behind an interface were considered and rejected for now: much larger churn across store and tests without removing caller knowledge. Revisit only if the union grows past ~30 fields.
- Special fields become per-field closures: signs (space strip), numerator/denominator (parseCoefficients), approximation (int).
- `validateBlockUpdate` (catalog.go:291) iterates definition fields; it calls the field's own set afterward.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `setParameter` and `parameterText` are gone; no switch on parameter name remains in the package.
- Adding a scalar parameter to a block touches only the Parameters struct and that block's definition entry.
- Behavior identical: same validation messages for malformed numbers, coefficients, signs, and Padé order; catalog_test.go passes unmodified.

- gofmt -w cmd internal && go vet ./...
- go test -race ./...
- go build ./cmd/processlab

Per-field numeric bounds should move onto the field definitions: today `bounded("gain", -10000, 10000)` restates the field's Min/Max editor strings — make the numeric bound the one authority and derive the editor attributes from it. The validate hook then carries only cross-field rules (transfer proper-ness, sign alphabet, Padé range).

- Add to `blockDefinition`: a role (source | dynamic | sink), `realize func(Block, inputs int) (*controlsys.System, error)`, and for sources `waveform func(Parameters, t float64) float64`.
- Sources and sinks realize as unit gains today (simulate.go:268-269); make that the default when realize is nil.
- Signal naming (sourceSignalName/inputSignalName/outputSignalName) stays in simulate.go — it is the compiler's concern, not the block's.
- The realize hook returns *controlsys.System because that is what this compiler consumes. Do not generalize the signature for hypothetical nonlinear engines; the engine spike (root task) owns that question.
- Consider splitting catalog.go into per-category files (sources.go, continuous.go, ...) if it passes ~700 lines; each block entry should read as one self-contained declaration.

## Acceptance Criteria
- simulate.go contains no switch over BlockKind.
- Each block's definition entry is self-contained: metadata, fields, defaults, validation, summary, realization or waveform in one place.
- simulate_test.go analytic-response tests pass unmodified (identical numerics).

## Validation Gates
- gofmt -w cmd internal && go vet ./... && go test -race ./... && go build ./cmd/processlab

data.title: Make the catalog the one authority for input arity
data.body:
## Goal
- State each block's input arity (none / exactly one / variadic) once, in its definition, and have both `Studio.Connect` (studio.go:383) and `compileFlow` (simulate.go:190) consult it.

## Context

## Acceptance Criteria

- Connect and compileFlow reject the same situations with the same messages as before; studio_test.go and simulate_test.go pass unmodified.

## Validation Gates

data.title: Retire the legacy scalar block columns
data.body:
## Goal
- Make `parameters_json` the only stored parameter representation, ending the era where every block insert and scan carries `amplitude`, `gain`, `time_constant` plus a JSON fallback.

## Context
- Add a startup migration in internal/studio/store.go that backfills parameters_json for rows where it is '' using the legacy scalars (the mapping is decodeParameters' switch, store.go:605-622). Afterward drop: decodeParameters' legacy branch, the three extra bind parameters in AddBlock (studio.go:65), DuplicateBlocks (studio.go:317), and seed (store.go:395), and the legacy scan columns (store.go:471, store.go:576).
- Keep the physical columns for old databases (SQLite column drops need table rebuilds for no upside); simply stop reading and writing them. New databases may omit them from CREATE TABLE — both a fresh db and a legacy one must open.
- register_test.go exercises legacy migration; extend it with a pre-JSON fixture whose scalar parameters must survive the backfill intact through a Snapshot.

## Acceptance Criteria
- No SQL outside the migration mentions amplitude, gain, or time_constant.
- A database from before parameters_json opens, backfills once, and shows identical block parameters; a second open does not rewrite rows.

## Validation Gates
- gofmt -w cmd internal && go vet ./... && go test -race ./... && go build ./cmd/processlab

data.title: Port-identified connections
Model ports in the domain and schema
data.body:
## Goal
- Give connections port identity — source_port and target_port — and give each block kind a port list, so multi-input blocks stop being a BlockSum special case and MIMO or subsystem blocks become expressible.

## Context
- Ports derive from the definition and the block's parameters: Sum exposes one input port per sign character; every other current block exposes at most one input and one output (port 0). Expose e.g. `Definition.InputPorts(parameters)`.
- Schema: connections gains source_port and target_port INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0. UNIQUE(flow_id, source_id, target_id) must become per-port; SQLite constraint changes need a create-copy-drop-rename table rebuild inside one transaction (same discipline as ensureProjects in store.go).
- Backfill: existing inbound Sum connections are numbered onto ports by connection id ascending — exactly the order compileFlow assigns signs today, so no stored model changes meaning.
- Domain rules, each an explicit refusal in the existing style: an input port holds at most one wire; a connection must name a port the block has; shrinking Sum's signs below its highest connected port is refused (no silent wire dropping).
- Connect (studio.go:383) gains port arguments; the HTTP handler reads optional source_port/target_port form values defaulting to 0, so the existing client keeps working until the workbench task lands.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Old databases migrate: every connection lands on port 0 except Sum inputs, which occupy ports 0..n-1 in connection-id order; re-opening does not renumber.
- Editing Sum signs refuses to orphan a wired port, with a message naming the port.
- Two wires into one input port are refused; wires into different ports of one block succeed.

## Validation Gates
- gofmt -w cmd internal && go vet ./... && go test -race ./... && go build ./cmd/processlab

data.title: Compile wiring by port
data.body:
## Goal
- Make the compiler wire signals by (block, port) instead of bare block id, so Sum signs bind to ports rather than to connection-id order.

## Context
- compileFlow (simulate.go) currently sorts Sum's incoming connections by connection id and matches signs positionally — deleting and redrawing a wire silently changes which sign it gets. After this task, sign i belongs to port i whatever order the wires were drawn.
- inputSignalName becomes port-qualified (block_N_input_P); realize hooks receive the connected ports; controlsys.Connection entries map source (id, port) to target (id, port).
- The seeded reactor model and every analytic simulate_test.go result must be numerically identical — the previous task's backfill guarantees sign assignments carry over.

## Acceptance Criteria
- A Sum with signs "+-" applies + to the wire on port 0 and - to port 1 regardless of creation order (add a test drawing them in reverse).
- Existing analytic response tests pass unmodified.

## Validation Gates
- gofmt -w cmd internal && go vet ./... && go test -race ./... && go build ./cmd/processlab

data.title: Render and wire ports in the workbench
data.body:
## Goal
- Draw each block's real ports and let wiring gestures name the port they touch, so a Sum shows one input pip per sign and a wire lands on the port the user chose.

## Context
- Template: workbench.html renders one input and one output button today (data-input-port keyed by block id). Ports become a per-block list on the view model; attributes carry block id plus port index. Edge paths (edgePath in view.go and its client twin) anchor at the port's y-offset instead of the block's vertical midline — the two implementations must stay geometrically identical.
- Design: stay inside the established instrument language (app.css tokens). Input pips distribute evenly along the block's left edge, outputs along the right; --signal orange remains outputs-only, inputs stay gray. The Sum block draws its sign character beside each pip — the sign on the sheet is the port label, exactly as the paper notation writes it. No new colors; aria-labels name block and port.
- JS: the wiring gestures (beginConnection/finishConnection in the gesture layer) and their htmx form values gain the two port fields; the draft edge snaps to the hovered pip.
- Inspector: the per-block connection list names the port (for Sum, the sign) so a model is legible without counting wires.

## Acceptance Criteria
- A Sum with signs "+-" renders two labeled input pips; dragging a wire onto each lands on that port; the persisted connection carries it; a full reload draws identical geometry (server path and client redraw agree).
- Single-port blocks look and behave exactly as before at 25%, 100%, and 400% zoom.

## Validation Gates
- gofmt -w cmd internal && go vet ./... && go test -race ./... && go build ./cmd/processlab
- Real pointer gestures over CDP against headless Chrome: wire to each Sum port, reload, verify persisted geometry (docs/workbench-ergonomics.md's pass is the model).

data.title: Verify and document the port model
data.body:
## Goal
- One end-to-end pass proving ports across the stack, then bring README.md and docs/workbench-ergonomics.md up to date.

## Context
- The pass: open a legacy database → migration lands Sum wires on ports → edit signs (grow allowed, orphaning shrink refused) → rewire between ports in the browser → simulate → numerics identical to the pre-port run for the seeded model.
- Document the port model in README (Supported blocks and SQLite data sections) and the gesture changes in docs/workbench-ergonomics.md.

## Acceptance Criteria
- A written verification section records the checks run (browser and migration), in the repo's existing verification style.
- README no longer describes Sum signs as connection-order-dependent.

## Validation Gates

- The CDP browser pass above, recorded in the doc.

data.title: Scale the client layer
Split app.js into ES modules
data.body:
## Goal
- Break the 1,551-line IIFE in internal/web/static/app.js into native ES modules with explicit state, so the next canvas features (ports, subsystems) land in a file of their own instead of growing one closure.

## Context
- Modules, by the state they own: viewport (pan/zoom/fit/readouts), selection (set, marquee, selection bar), dragging (block drag, guides, nudge), wiring (ports, draft edge), shell (rails, dock, shortcut sheet, persistence), plus a small shared canvas-geometry module (geometry(), screenToSheet, edgePath — edgePath must keep matching its server-side twin in view.go).
- No bundler: script type="module" in page.html; files under static/js/ ride the existing go:embed and the CSP 'self' rule. menu.js, tabs.js, and register.js already load separately — leave them.
- The delicate part is the htmx re-apply contract: after every #workbench swap, viewport, selection, and shell state re-apply from localStorage. Keep one explicit re-apply entry point modules register with, replacing scattered htmx:afterSettle listeners.
- Pure reorganization: no behavior, key-map, or persistence-key changes.

## Acceptance Criteria
- No module reaches into another's mutable state except through exported functions; each file under ~400 lines.
- The documented gesture set works unchanged — verified with the CDP interaction pass at 25%, 100%, and 400% zoom (viewport, snapping, marquee, keyboard, context menus, wiring).

## Validation Gates
- go build ./cmd/processlab (embed picks up the new files)
- go test -race ./... (embedded-asset tests)
- CDP pass over the workbench gestures.

data.title: spike: measure workbench swap cost at scale
data.body:
## Goal
- Learn where the full-#workbench-swap architecture actually stops scaling, so any move to finer-grained swaps is decided on numbers, not fear.

## Context
- Every mutation re-renders and swaps the whole workbench fragment, then re-applies client state. At the seeded 8 blocks this is instant; nobody has measured 100 or 400.
- Method: script databases with 50-, 150-, and 400-block flowsheets (grid-placed, chained); measure server render time, fragment size, and browser swap+settle+re-apply time over CDP for a block move and a parameter edit at each size, at 25% and 100% zoom.

## Acceptance Criteria
- docs/swap-scaling.md with the numbers and one recommendation: either "full swap holds to N blocks; revisit at N" or the concrete shape of follow-up work (for example: oob-swap the inspector, dock, and tabs; patch block cards in place). What dependent tasks must learn: the block-count budget and the recommended swap strategy.
- The measurement script is checked in beside the doc and runnable by another agent.

## Validation Gates
- Doc and script exist; script runs against a scratch database without touching processlab.db.

data.title: Share one design-token stylesheet
data.body:
## Goal
- Move the :root token block that app.css and register.css each carry into one tokens.css both pages link, so the palette has one authority instead of a copied block and a comment promising the copies match.

## Context
- register.css:1-18 documents the copy as deliberate isolation from the 3,000-line canvas stylesheet. The isolation is right; the copying is not. tokens.css holds exactly the shared :root block (and the shared dark-scheme override if both shells carry one); each page adds one link tag before its own stylesheet.
- app.css keeps workbench-only tokens. The register's rule that --signal orange never appears on it holds by the register never using the variable; it does not need a separate palette file.
- Templates: page.html and register.html gain the link tag; CSP stays 'self'; assets stay embedded.

## Acceptance Criteria
- One :root token definition in the repository; both pages render identically (spot-check register and workbench at 1280px, light and dark scheme, via CDP screenshots).
- register.css's header comment states the new arrangement.

## Validation Gates

- CDP screenshot spot-check.

data.title: Centralize model-edit bookkeeping in Studio
data.body:
## Goal
- State the rule "a model edit touches model_updated_at, a layout edit does not, every edit logs an event and stamps updated_at" once, instead of ten times.

## Context
- Every mutation in internal/studio/studio.go repeats the same coda: format now, UPDATE flows SET updated_at (plus model_updated_at for model edits), insertEvent, re-snapshot — AddBlock, UpdateBlock, DeleteBlock(s), DuplicateBlocks, Connect, Disconnect(s), MoveBlock(s). Which operations count as model edits is the invariant behind the amber staleness dot, and it currently lives in the copies.
- Shape: an unexported helper (for example s.mutateFlow(ctx, flowID, modelEdit bool, event string, fn)) or two flavors (modelEdit / layoutEdit) if that reads better — MoveBlocks stamps updated_at only and logs no event, and the helper must express that without a flag explosion. Pick the smallest shape that removes the copies while each operation keeps owning its SQL.

## Acceptance Criteria
- The updated_at / model_updated_at / event coda appears once per flavor; every mutation goes through it.
- studio_test.go and lifecycle_test.go pass unmodified; staleness-dot behavior is untouched (register_test.go).

## Validation Gates
- gofmt -w cmd internal && go vet ./... && go test -race ./... && go build ./cmd/processlab

data.title: spike: chart a discrete and nonlinear engine path
data.body:
## Goal
- Decide, on paper, how Process Lab grows past the linear boundary — Unit Delay, discrete filters, Product, Saturation, Switch, Relay — so block work after the catalog container can be scheduled with real dependencies.

## Context
- Today the compiler composes LTI realizations via controlsys.ConnectByName + Lsim (internal/studio/simulate.go); README states the linear boundary deliberately.
- Questions to answer: (1) what controlsys v1.2.0 offers beyond Lsim (discrete systems, nonlinear stepping); (2) a mixed sample-time policy for discrete blocks; (3) whether nonlinear blocks need a per-step graph evaluator (fixed-step integration over the topological order compileFlow already computes) beside the LTI path, and how the two coexist on one sheet; (4) which block families each investment unlocks, in dependency order.
- Integration point: the catalog realize hook (after "Move realization and waveforms into the catalog") is where a second engine would attach a different realization; propose that seam without building it.

## Acceptance Criteria
- docs/simulation-engine-roadmap.md: options with tradeoffs, one recommendation, and a dependency-ordered block/engine task list ready to file into ergo.
- What dependent tasks must learn from this spike: the chosen engine strategy and the order block families become possible. File the recommended follow-up tasks into ergo, or state explicitly that none are filed yet.

data.title: spike: design hierarchical subsystems
data.body:
## Goal
- Produce the design for subsystem blocks — a flowsheet inside a block, the signature Simulink structure README currently rules out — so implementation can be planned as ordinary tasks.

## Context
- Questions: data model (a subsystem block referencing a child flow, versus flows nesting via a parent block id; which project the child sheet belongs to; cascade rules on delete and duplicate), port surface (child Inport/Outport blocks becoming the parent block ports — requires port identity, delivered by the ports container), navigation (tab strip versus breadcrumb descent; canonical URLs), and compilation (inline the child graph into the parent before compileFlow, with namespaced signal names).
- Constraints worth honoring from this codebase: every list the UI draws has one query authority; refusals are explicit domain messages; migrations open old databases unchanged.

## Acceptance Criteria
- docs/subsystem-design.md answering the questions with one recommendation and a task breakdown ready for ergo.
- Explicitly lists what stays out of a first subsystem release (masked parameters, library links, and similar).

## Scope
- Make one catalog entry the single authority for everything a block kind is: metadata, fields, defaults, parsing, validation, summary, arity, realization. Adding a Simulink-style block should be one definition in one file plus tests.

## Non-goals
- No new blocks in this container; it changes where knowledge lives, not what exists.
- No nonlinear or discrete engine work (see the engine spike at root).
- No port identity (next container).

## Decisions
- Keep the flat Parameters union struct and the JSON wire format; behavior moves into definitions as typed closures. Per-kind parameter structs behind an interface were rejected: large churn without removing caller knowledge. Revisit past ~30 union fields.
- Validation message text is a compatibility surface for tests and the interface; preserve it.

## Evidence
- Adding a block today touches ~8 sites: BlockKind consts and Parameters fields (model.go); blockOrder, blockDefinitions, setParameter, parameterText, validateParameters, Summary (catalog.go); realizeBlock, sourceValue, isSource/isSink, the arity walk (simulate.go); and the Connect arity check (studio.go).

## Scope
- Port identity end to end: schema, domain rules, compiler, workbench UI. The enabling move for Product, Switch, Mux, MIMO State-Space, and subsystem Inport/Outport blocks — none of which are built here.

## Non-goals
- No new block kinds. No block uses more than one output port yet (the model supports it).

## Decisions
- Port lists derive from definition plus parameters (Sum: one input port per sign). Port 0 is the default, so existing rows and clients stay valid mid-container.
- Shrinking Sum signs below a wired port is refused, not silently disconnected.
- Migration numbers existing Sum inputs by connection id, preserving the compiled meaning of every stored model exactly.

## Constraints
- Depends on the catalog container: arity and roles must already live in definitions before ports generalize them.

## Scope
- Keep the framework-free client architecture viable as canvas features multiply: modular gesture code, a measured swap budget, one token authority.

## Non-goals
- No bundler, no framework, no TypeScript — "embedded, framework-free" is the stack constraint and it stays.
- No visual redesign; the workbench design system is settled and documented in docs/workbench-ergonomics.md.

data.title: Deepen the controlsys model core

data.body:
## Goal
- Make the Studio compiler expose one cohesive, named control-system model that delegates interconnection, feedback, signal identity, and numerical validation to `controlsys`.

## Scope
- Recover the stashed native-feedback work as the first implementation input.
- Keep persisted block and wire intent in Studio while `controlsys.System` owns numerical composition.
- Preserve stable block/port identities while carrying human-readable input, output, state, and analysis-point names.

## Non-goals
- Do not pattern-match arbitrary graphs into `Series`, `Parallel`, or `Feedback`; `ConnectByName` remains the general graph operation.
- Do not duplicate control algorithms, frequency-response calculations, or delay solvers in the application.
- Do not expose `controlsys` mutable structs directly through HTTP or persistence.

## Decisions
- The compiler returns a deep internal compiled-model artifact, not a growing tuple of systems, maps, and ordering slices.
- Algebraic-loop failures come from composition and are translated once at the Studio boundary.
- The linear path remains exact for the model the user drew; there is no silent linearization or approximation.

Unresolved questions: none

data.title: Integrate native feedback and algebraic-loop diagnostics
data.body:
## Goal
- Restore the named stash `WIP: controlsys-native feedback for full toolbox integration`, retain valid dynamic feedback, and translate only genuinely unsolvable algebraic loops into a domain error.

## Context
- Start from the stash; do not reconstruct it from memory.
- `Studio.Connect` validates diagram ports and occupancy. It must not reject a cycle merely because it is a cycle.
- `compileFlow` delegates the complete graph to `controlsys.ConnectByName`.

## Acceptance Criteria
- A setpoint -> Sum(+-) -> PID -> plant loop simulates and agrees sample-for-sample with an independent `controlsys.Series` plus `controlsys.Feedback` oracle.
- A singular direct-feedthrough algebraic loop is refused with an actionable Studio message.
- Valid branching, merging, multi-source, and acyclic models remain numerically unchanged.
- README and roadmap statements no longer claim all cycles are rejected.

## Validation Gates
- `gofmt -w cmd internal`
- `go vet ./...`
- `go test -race ./...`
- `go build ./cmd/processlab`

data.title: Own a named compiled-model artifact
data.body:
## Goal
- Replace the compiler's shallow system/sources/sinks tuple with one internal artifact that owns the composed `controlsys.System`, source excitations, diagram-to-signal identity, selected outputs, and model provenance.

## Context
- Callers should ask to compile a flowsheet for simulation or analysis without coordinating naming, output exposure, validation, or selection order.
- Block and port IDs remain persistence identities; signal names are derived once at compilation.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Simulation has one intent-revealing compile call and no caller-managed naming or channel-order sequence.
- Every external input and output has a stable controlsys name plus its block/port identity.
- The artifact can expose dimensions, time domain, and selected channels without leaking mutable matrices.
- Existing persisted runs and HTTP contracts remain compatible.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./internal/studio`
- `go vet ./...`
- `go build ./cmd/processlab`

data.title: Expose named internal signals and analysis probes
data.body:
## Goal
- Let simulation and analysis request arbitrary diagram signals by block/port identity while the compiler decides which controlsys outputs must remain externally visible.

## Context
- `ConnectByName` can expose only the outputs named at composition time; internal signals cannot be recovered after elimination.
- Scope blocks are one consumer of signals, not the authority on which signals may be inspected.

## Acceptance Criteria
- A compile request names desired source, sink, or internal block-port signals without spelling controlsys strings.
- Duplicate probes are coalesced and returned in deterministic request order.
- `SelectByName` is used where selection occurs after composition; otherwise requested outputs are included in the `ConnectByName` output set.
- Named input/output metadata survives composition and response generation.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./internal/studio`
- Numerical tests cover a branched feedback model with probes before and after the loop.

data.title: Lock the interconnection numerical contract
data.body:
## Goal
- Add persistent independent checks proving the general compiler matches controlsys's specialized algebra across representative SISO and MIMO graph shapes.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Oracles cover series, parallel, signed sums, dynamic feedback, multiple external inputs, multiple selected outputs, and direct feedthrough.
- Tests compare full sampled responses and model dimensions, names, poles, and DC gains where defined.
- Ill-posed algebraic loops, duplicate names, dimension mismatches, and mixed time domains fail deterministically.
- A compile benchmark records scaling by block, state, and connection count without imposing a premature performance threshold.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./internal/studio`
- `go test ./internal/studio -run '^$' -bench 'Compile|Connect' -benchmem`

data.title: Deliver control-system analysis and diagnostics

data.body:
## Goal
- Turn a compiled flowsheet into a control-engineering workspace using controlsys time, frequency, pole-zero, stability, and robustness analyses.

## Scope
- Analysis is requested against named inputs, outputs, and explicit loop breaks.
- Studio owns request validation and presentation models; controlsys owns calculations.

## Non-goals
- A signal FFT is not presented as a Bode plot.
- Step-response metrics are not attached to arbitrary sine or multi-source runs.
- Closed-loop transfer functions are not used to report open-loop margins without an explicit loop break.

## Decisions
- Analysis results record the model revision and selected named channels.
- Numerical result types remain internal; HTTP views receive immutable presentation data.

Unresolved questions: none

data.title: Add stability, pole-zero, gain, damping, and step diagnostics
data.body:
## Goal
- Expose `Poles`, `Zeros`, `IsStable`, `DCGain`, `Damp`, and standard step-response metrics for selected compiled channels.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Step analysis uses `controlsys.Step` and `StepInfo` only for a declared step experiment.
- Rise time, settling time, overshoot, undershoot, peak, peak time, steady-state value, stability, poles, zeros, and damping are represented.
- Undefined, unstable, improper, or non-SISO operations produce useful partial results or domain errors rather than NaN-filled UI.
- Existing arbitrary-input run metrics remain clearly separate.

## Validation Gates
- Oracle tests against analytically known first- and second-order systems.
- `go test -race ./internal/studio ./internal/web`

data.title: Add Bode, Nyquist, Nichols, and singular-value analysis
data.body:
## Goal
- Compute model frequency responses through controlsys for named SISO and MIMO channel selections.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Automatic and explicit frequency grids are supported.
- SISO results include Bode, Nyquist, and Nichols data; MIMO results include singular values.
- Frequency units, magnitude units, phase unwrap policy, and discrete Nyquist limits have one authority.
- The existing Spectrum Analyzer remains a sampled-signal FFT and is labeled distinctly.

## Validation Gates
- Compare selected points with analytic transfer functions and independent complex evaluation.
- `go test -race ./internal/studio ./internal/web`

data.title: Add loop margins, bandwidth, root locus, and passivity diagnostics
data.body:
## Goal
- Analyze an explicitly selected loop using `Margin`, `AllMargin`, `DiskMargin`, `Bandwidth`, `RootLocus`, and sampled passivity evidence where applicable.

## Context
- The task depends on named probes but must not invent a loop from topology heuristics.

## Acceptance Criteria
- A user identifies the loop input/output or analysis point by diagram signal identity.
- Gain, phase, disk margins, crossover frequencies, bandwidth, and root-locus data are returned with applicability metadata.
- MIMO and sampled-data limitations are stated by the operation rather than hidden in the UI.
- Passivity results are labeled sampled evidence, not an analytic certificate.

## Validation Gates
- Reference cases cover stable, unstable, no-crossover, multiple-crossover, and discrete loops.
- `go test -race ./internal/studio`

data.title: Build the analysis workspace and revision-aware results
data.body:
## Goal
- Add a cohesive analysis surface for choosing named channels, running analyses, and comparing results without turning handlers into orchestration scripts.

## Acceptance Criteria
- One Studio operation owns validation, compilation, calculation, persistence or ephemeral caching, and stale-result rules per analysis intent.
- Time, Bode, Nyquist, Nichols, singular-value, pole-zero, root-locus, and metric views share channel/revision metadata.
- Editing the model visibly marks prior analysis stale.
- Keyboard, responsive layout, and HTMX swaps retain existing workbench behavior.

data.title: Route flowsheet signals like Simulink
data.body:
## Goal
- Deliver Simulink-like signal routing for the flowsheet so forward and feedback connections remain readable as blocks move.

## Scope
- Replace cubic curves with deterministic orthogonal routes.
- Keep source and target ports authoritative.
- Avoid block cards and reduce avoidable overlap between signals.
- Preserve HTMX redraw, block dragging, and draft wiring behavior.

## Non-goals
- Automatic block placement.
- Signal branching or editable manual bend points.
- Changes to simulation or connection persistence.

## Decisions
- One pure client routing module owns route computation; Go renders connection topology and port geometry only.
- Use obstacle-aware rectilinear routing with fixed port exits, block clearance, bend penalties, and prior-edge occupancy penalties.
- Prefer left-to-right paths; route right-to-left feedback around the diagram when needed.

## Validation
- Persistent JavaScript algorithm tests.
- Focused and full Go test suites, race test, vet, build, and diff checks.
- Browser verification of the seeded PID feedback model during drag and after reload.

data.title: Build the orthogonal routing engine
data.body:
## Goal

## Context

## Acceptance Criteria
- Every segment is horizontal or vertical.
- Routes do not enter inflated block rectangles except at their own port stubs.
- Forward routes use the direct channel when clear.
- Feedback routes leave the source to the right and enter the target from the left without cubic loops.
- Deterministic tie-breaking and occupancy costs separate avoidable shared segments.
- A fallback route remains orthogonal if no graph path is available.

spike: reproduce freezes and establish performance budgets
data.body:
## Goal

## Context

- Re-check those conclusions after the orthogonal-routing and rebrand changes; stale numbers are not implementation authority.
- Preserve the full-workbench server-rendered cards-and-wires invariant and the benchmark's raw/numeric/negative-control route checks.
- TypeScript is not itself a performance optimization. Only adopt a new asset build step if measured load or transfer results justify it without losing the Go-only runnable artifact.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Run the current benchmark at representative small and large flowsheets using real headless Chrome.
- Capture parameter-edit latency, reapply time, settle wait, redraw/drag frame time, page load, response bytes, compressed bytes, and route-correctness controls.
- Reproduce or bound the unresponsive behavior at 400 or 640 blocks, including a constrained-CPU profile if normal headless Chrome does not expose it.

data.title: eliminate redundant full-swap client work
data.body:

## Context

- Preserve redraws for browser-local movement such as dragging, keyboard nudging, resize, and any future partial swap that can make cards and wires disagree.
- Use the budgets and attribution written by the baseline spike.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Initial load and full-workbench swaps do not call route recomputation when server-rendered paths are authoritative.
- HTMX does not pay an unused settle delay; application reapply behavior remains correct after swaps and history restore.
- The benchmark reports zero numeric route differences for every full-swap interaction and a non-zero negative control.
- Parameter edits meet the concrete 400-block latency budget recorded by the baseline spike.
- Add persistent regression coverage for the server-rendered route authority and HTMX configuration.

## Validation Gates

- Focused `go test ./internal/web`

data.title: compress and cache application delivery safely
data.body:
## Goal
- Remove avoidable network cost for large HTMX fragments and embedded static assets without mixing representations or caching private state.

## Context
- Current dynamic fragments are served uncompressed; the existing 400-block measurement is approximately 427.7 KiB raw versus 25.6 KiB gzipped.
- Full pages and HTMX fragments can share URLs, so `Vary` and cache rules must prevent a fragment from occupying a full-page cache entry.
- The app remains self-contained with locally embedded HTMX and assets.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Eligible HTML, CSS, JavaScript, JSON, and SVG responses negotiate compression correctly.
- `HEAD`, 204, already encoded, incompressible, and small responses retain correct semantics.
- Responses vary on `Accept-Encoding`; full/fragment routes retain correct `Vary: HX-Request` behavior.
- Versioned immutable assets receive long-lived caching; mutable page assets and private workbench data do not receive unsafe shared caching.
- Persistent HTTP tests cover negotiation, headers, body integrity, and HTMX representation separation.
- The large-fragment transfer meets the concrete network budget recorded by the baseline spike.

## Validation Gates
- `go test ./internal/web`
- `go test -race ./internal/web`
- Focused HTTP compression and cache tests
- Large-sheet benchmark with compressed-response reporting

data.title: verify scale, document evidence, and prepare release
data.body:
## Goal
- Prove the refactor improves responsiveness across representative scale and leaves a repeatable performance gate for future changes.

## Context
- Compare against the baseline produced by the spike, not historical projections.
- Full-swap refinement or partial swaps are allowed only if the post-fix profile still misses the accepted budget and the route-authority invariant is repaired in the same change.
- Preserve the fast-web principles: server-rendered useful HTML, explicit page assets, local dependencies, stable layout, and measured cold/warm/constrained profiles.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Run the full benchmark at 50, 150, 400, and 640 blocks, including both supported zoom levels and a constrained profile.
- Document before/after medians, tails, payloads, route controls, and remaining limits in `docs/swap-scaling.md`.
- No measured interaction exceeds the budgets established by the baseline spike without a documented, evidence-backed reason and follow-up task.
- Validate real browser drag, parameter edit, reload, history, project register, and responsive viewport behavior.
- Run the complete Go, Node, race, vet, build, formatting, diff, and Docker/config gates relevant to the repository.

## Validation Gates
- `node --test internal/web/static/js/*_test.js`
- `go test -race -count=1 ./...`
- `go vet ./...`
- `go build ./...`
- `gofmt -l .`
- `git diff --check`
- `docker compose config --quiet`
- Full benchmark and real-browser checks documented in `docs/swap-scaling.md`

## Goal
- Reduce every full-workbench interaction to one required client routing pass and reuse authoritative cached paths when the flow layout and topology are unchanged.

## Context
- The current server intentionally emits empty SVG `d` attributes. `orthogonal-routing.js` is the route authority, so the original recommendation to remove all swap redraws is invalid.
- `reapply.js` currently runs every step after both `htmx:afterSwap` and `htmx:afterSettle`. Its own contract says the afterSwap query can still resolve the node HTMX is discarding; the settled pass is the one that sticks.
- The repaired benchmark proves normal afterSwap and afterSettle routes are identical, while its displaced-card negative control changes two paths.
- A parameter edit does not change flow ID, block geometry, ports, edges, or obstacle layout. The module-level route cache survives the DOM swap and can populate the replacement SVG without rebuilding visibility graphs.
- Use the 2026-08-02 baseline and budgets in `docs/swap-scaling.md`.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Initial load, one settled full-workbench swap, and history restore produce complete non-empty routes.
- The application does not reroute the discarded afterSwap DOM.
- HTMX settle delay is zero because the application defines no settling transition.
- A stable layout/topology signature lets parameter edits, selection, simulation, and equivalent swaps reuse cached paths while filling the replacement SVG in O(edges).
- Flow switches, changed endpoints, moved/added/deleted blocks, and added/deleted edges invalidate only what can no longer be trusted; reload and live geometry remain deterministic.
- The route-authority benchmark is revised so it remains a valid falsifiable gate after the duplicate pass is removed.
- The 400-block parameter edit reaches the accepted median-to-frame budget of at most 150 ms, with 100 ms as the stretch target.
- Persistent Node and Go tests cover the lifecycle configuration, cache reuse, and invalidation behavior.

## Validation Gates
- `node --test internal/web/static/js/*_test.js`
- `go test ./internal/web`
- `node docs/swap-scaling-bench.mjs --sizes 50 --server-reps 5 --swap-reps 2 --load-reps 2`
- `node docs/swap-scaling-bench.mjs --sizes 400 --server-reps 5 --swap-reps 2 --load-reps 2 --skip-profile --skip-redundancy`
- `git diff --check`

## Goal
- Make the authoritative initial route build and browser-local geometry updates fast enough to stay interactive at 400 blocks.

## Context
- The baseline identifies `buildVisibilityGraph` and `segmentCrossesRect` as the dominant functions. The current router creates the Cartesian product of every obstacle x/y boundary separately for every edge.
- At 400 blocks, one route pass takes 3.35–3.47 seconds. At 150 blocks, parameter edits and drags already create 200–307 ms long tasks.
- Build per-call block/edge indexes instead of whole-canvas selector scans per edge.
- Prefer deterministic collision-free Manhattan candidates and a bounded fallback over a per-edge unbounded Cartesian visibility graph. Preserve obstacle clearance, port stubs, feedback routing, crossing/overlap penalties where they materially choose among valid candidates, and deterministic ordering.
- Preserve route cache and requestAnimationFrame batching. If a full obstacle-aware reroute cannot meet the frame budget during drag, use cheap provisional paths during pointer movement and one authoritative route build on release.

## Acceptance Criteria
- The normal flowsheet path avoids constructing an obstacle-coordinate Cartesian product per edge.
- A complete 400-edge route pass is at most 150 ms on the baseline host.
- Drag routing produces no long task above 50 ms at 400 blocks and does not lose live pointer moves.
- A 4× CPU-slowdown run has no routing task above 250 ms.
- Route output remains orthogonal, deterministic, within bounds, and clear of block obstacles for forward, feedback, blocked-stub, multichannel-port, and dense-layout cases.
- Reload, add, delete, connect, disconnect, drag, nudge, and resize retain correct cache invalidation and stable paths.
- Add persistent oracle-style geometry tests for every new fast-path/fallback rule and regression.

## Validation Gates
- `node --test internal/web/static/js/*_test.js`
- `go test ./internal/web`
- `node docs/swap-scaling-bench.mjs --sizes 50,150,400 --server-reps 5 --swap-reps 3 --load-reps 2 --skip-redundancy`
- `node docs/swap-scaling-bench.mjs --sizes 150 --server-reps 2 --swap-reps 2 --load-reps 1 --cpu-slowdown 4 --skip-profile --skip-redundancy`
- `git diff --check`

## Goal
- Negotiate compression and safe cache policy so large HTMX fragments and embedded assets do not waste network time.

## Context
- The current 400-block fragment is 645.8 KiB raw and 28.6 KiB with gzip, while the loopback server completes the PUT in about 26 ms.
- Full pages and HTMX fragments can share URLs, so `Vary` and cache rules must prevent representation mixing.
- The app remains self-contained with locally embedded HTMX and assets.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Eligible HTML, CSS, JavaScript, JSON, and SVG responses negotiate gzip correctly and a client that does not advertise gzip receives the original body.
- `HEAD`, 204, already encoded, incompressible, and small responses retain correct status, length, and body semantics.
- Compressed responses append `Accept-Encoding` to `Vary`; full/fragment routes retain `Vary: HX-Request` without either value overwriting the other.
- The versioned HTMX asset receives long-lived immutable caching. Mutable application assets and private workbench data do not receive unsafe shared caching.
- Persistent HTTP tests cover negotiation quality values, wildcard/identity behavior, header composition, decompressed body integrity, and HTMX representation separation.
- The 400-block dynamic HTML transfer is at most 35 KiB when gzip is negotiated.

## Validation Gates
- `go test ./internal/web`
- `go test -race ./internal/web`
- Focused compression and cache tests
- `node docs/swap-scaling-bench.mjs --sizes 400 --server-reps 5 --swap-reps 1 --load-reps 1 --skip-profile --skip-redundancy`
- `git diff --check`

data.title: Align vector and routing behavior
data.body:
## Goal
- Distinguish direct Simulink vector semantics from Process-Lab-specific named-channel routing and close the highest-value gaps.

## Context
- Mux, Demux, Selector, Permutation, Vector Constant, Vector Sum, Matrix Gain, and Vector Scope include Process-Lab-specific named-channel abstractions.

## Goal
- Extend draft PR #10 with staged Process Lab block-layer compatibility against official MathWorks R2026a online documentation.

## Decisions
- Treat controlsys v1.3.0 as the faithful Control System Toolbox foundation; close adapter, default, editor, persistence, and public-behavior gaps in Process Lab.
- Keep First-Order Lag as a simple composable lag and model dead time with Transport Delay.
- Preserve the existing workbench, saved-diagram schema, no-delay fast path, and named-channel abstractions unless a scoped direct-block requirement needs a targeted additive change.
- Expected values use documented examples, analytic equations, or controlsys oracles with explicit provenance; none are described as MATLAB output.

## Priority
- First: direct scalar defaults and initial-state/history contracts.
- Next: state-space vectors and Transport Delay history.
- Then: PID form/parameter semantics.
- Then: direct vector behavior while retaining Process-Lab-specific routing blocks.

## Non-goals
