data.title: processlab CLI foundation and JSON transport
Restructure the processlab binary around subcommands
data.body:
## Goal
- Turn `cmd/processlab` from a single-purpose server launcher into a subcommand
  dispatcher, so every later command plugs into one argv, usage, and exit-code
  contract instead of restating it.

## Context
- Today `cmd/processlab/main.go` parses `-addr` and `-db` with the `flag`
  package and immediately serves. That behaviour moves to `processlab serve`
  with the same two flags, same defaults (`127.0.0.1:8080`, `processlab.db`),
  and the same graceful-shutdown path.
- Bare `processlab` prints the command list and exits 2. This is a deliberate
  breaking change; every launcher in the repository must move with it:
  `Dockerfile` (CMD), `compose.yaml`, `README.md` "Run it" and "Run with Docker
  Compose", and the browser suite's binary launch under `browser/`.
- Use the standard library only. No cobra, no urfave/cli. The command tree is a
  Go value, not a framework registration, because task A4 serves that same
  value as machine-readable help.
- One command is one struct holding name, one-line summary, flag registration,
  and run function. The dispatcher owns argv splitting, `--help` on any command,
  unknown-command errors, and exit codes. A command body never calls
  `os.Exit`, never writes usage text, and never touches `flag.CommandLine`.

## Decisions
- Streams: data on stdout, diagnostics and errors on stderr. A command that
  produces no data writes nothing to stdout.
- Exit codes: 0 success, 1 the operation was rejected or failed, 2 usage error
  (unknown command, bad flag, missing required argument), 3 no Process Lab
  server could be reached. A skill branches on these, so they are contract.
- Global flags, defined once by the dispatcher: `--server` (default
  `http://127.0.0.1:8080`, env `PROCESSLAB_ADDR`), `--json`, `--help`.
  `--db` belongs to `serve` alone; no client command opens SQLite.
- Colour and column alignment only when stdout is a terminal and `NO_COLOR` is
  unset. Piped output is plain and stable.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `processlab serve --addr 127.0.0.1:0 --db <tmp>` serves the existing web
  application unchanged and shuts down on SIGTERM as it does today.
- `processlab` with no arguments prints the command list to stderr, exit 2.
- `processlab nosuchthing` names the unknown command on stderr, exit 2.
- `processlab --help` and `processlab serve --help` print usage to stdout,
  exit 0. Help is never an error when asked for explicitly.
- `PROCESSLAB_ADDR` is read when `--server` is absent; `--server` wins when
  both are present.
- `docker compose up` still serves the application; the browser suite still
  launches a server and passes.

## Validation Gates
- `gofmt -l cmd internal` prints nothing
- `go vet ./...`
- `go test -race ./...`
- `go build ./cmd/processlab`
- `npm run test:browser`

data.title: Add the /api/v1 JSON envelope and error contract
data.body:
## Goal
- Give the server one JSON surface with one error shape, so every later
  endpoint and every CLI command inherits a single decoding, status-mapping,
  and failure vocabulary rather than restating it per handler.

## Context
- The current handlers in `internal/web/server.go` render HTML fragments and
  call `s.renderFailure`, which turns any error into workbench markup. That is
  right for htmx and wrong for a client. Do not change it; add a sibling
  surface under `/api/v1/` registered on the same mux in `web.New`.
- `studio.ValidationMessage` (`internal/studio/studio.go:705`) already collapses
  `*studio.ValidationError` and `studio.ErrNotFound` into user text. The JSON
  surface needs the same collapse plus the distinction the HTML path throws
  away: which kind of failure it was.
- Only `exportResults` emits JSON today, at `GET /flows/{flowID}/results.json`.
  Leave that route in place; it is what the GUI's download button uses.

## Decisions
- Success body is the studio record encoded directly. The studio types already
  carry `json` tags (`AnalysisWorkspace`, `ResultsExport`, `ParameterSweep`,
  `IdentificationDataset`), so no parallel DTO layer is introduced. A type
  that must not leak a field fixes its own tags.
- Failure body is `{"error":{"kind":"...","message":"..."}}` where kind is one
  of `usage`, `not_found`, `conflict`, `internal`. Status mapping lives in one
  function: validation to 400, `ErrNotFound` to 404, registry conflicts to 409,
  anything else to 500 with a generic message and a server-side log.
- Requests carry JSON bodies with a size limit; form encoding is the GUI's
  business, not the API's.
- The API keeps the existing trust boundary: it binds where `serve` binds,
  loopback by default, and adds no authentication. Record that here so no
  later task invents a token scheme by accident.

## Acceptance Criteria
- A handler returning `&studio.ValidationError{}` produces 400 with kind
  `usage` and the validation message verbatim.
- A handler returning `studio.ErrNotFound` produces 404 with kind `not_found`.
- An unexpected error produces 500 with kind `internal`, a message that leaks
  no internals, and a log line that keeps the original.
- A request body over the limit is refused with 400 rather than read.
- A request with a non-JSON content type is refused with 400.
- Existing HTML routes and `results.json` are byte-for-byte unaffected; the
  existing `internal/web/server_test.go` suite passes untouched.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./internal/web/...`
- `go vet ./...`

data.title: Add the CLI HTTP client and end-to-end test harness
data.body:
## Goal
- Give client commands one way to reach the server and one way to be tested,
  so no later task hand-rolls request plumbing or its own fixture.

## Context
- Depends on the dispatcher and the JSON envelope. The client is the only
  place in `cmd/processlab` that knows about HTTP, URLs, or status codes; a
  command asks for a resource and receives a decoded record or an error.
- The failure a skill hits most is "no server". A refused connection must not
  surface as a Go transport error. It reads as: what address was tried, that
  nothing answered, and that `processlab serve` starts one. Exit 3.

## Decisions
- The client returns errors that carry the envelope's `kind`, and the
  dispatcher maps kind to exit code. A command never chooses an exit code.
- Timeouts are generous, not absent: synthesis and sweeps are slow. A single
  `--timeout` global flag with a default measured in minutes, and no timeout
  at all is not an option, so a wedged request cannot hang a skill forever.
- The harness builds the real binary once, starts a real server on port 0
  against a throwaway database, and runs commands as subprocesses. It asserts
  on stdout, stderr, and exit code separately. Every later command task adds
  cases to it; nothing in this repository tests a CLI by calling its run
  function directly, because the argv and stream contract is the thing under
  test.

## Acceptance Criteria
- A command against a closed port prints the attempted address and the
  `processlab serve` hint on stderr, nothing on stdout, exit 3.
- A 400 envelope prints its message on stderr, nothing on stdout, exit 1.
- A 500 envelope prints the generic message on stderr, exit 1.
- The harness starts a server, runs `processlab --server <addr> --help`, and
  tears down cleanly with no leaked process or temporary database.
- Harness output on failure shows the full command line, both streams, and the
  exit code.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./cmd/...`
- `go vet ./...`

data.title: Emit the command tree as machine-readable help
data.body:
## Goal
- Let a skill discover what this CLI can do without a human transcribing it,
  by serving the same command tree that `--help` renders as JSON.

## Context
- Depends on the dispatcher, whose command tree is already a Go value. This
  task adds a second rendering of that value, not a second copy of it. If a
  command's summary or flags can be stated anywhere other than its definition,
  this task has failed.
- Per-block parameter help is not here; the catalog owns that and task B3
  attaches it to the block subcommands. This task covers the tree: commands,
  their summaries, their flags, their arguments.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `processlab help --json` prints the full tree: every command and subcommand
  with name, summary, flags (name, type, default, description) and positional
  arguments, on stdout, exit 0.
- `processlab help <command> --json` prints that subtree.
- A command added in a later task appears in the JSON with no edit to this
  task's code. Prove it with a test that walks the tree and asserts every
  registered command is reachable and has a non-empty summary.
- Text `--help` and JSON help never disagree: one test renders both and
  compares the command names and flag names they contain.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./cmd/...`

data.title: Self-documenting block library and flowsheet authoring
Make the block catalog the single authority for parameter schema
data.body:
## Goal
- Publish, from the catalog, the full editable shape of a block kind: its
  fields with type, default, bounds, unit, options, help text, and its port
  structure. Without this, the CLI's per-block help is a second transcription
  of `internal/studio/catalog.go` that drifts the first time a bound changes.

## Context
- `blockDefinition.Parameters` (`internal/studio/catalog.go:118`) already holds
  every fact: `parameterDefinition` carries Name, Label, Type, Step, Min, Max,
  Unit, Placeholder, Help, Options, and a `bound` whose min and max are the
  same two numbers `validateBound` enforces. It is all unexported.
- The only way out today is `Block.EditorFields()` (`catalog.go:2416`), which
  needs a constructed `Block`. `BlockLibrary()` (`catalog.go:2375`) returns
  `BlockDefinition` with no fields at all. `internal/web/view.go:343` iterates
  the library and `view.go:357` calls `EditorFields` on an instance.
- Port structure has the same shape of problem: `Block.InputPort` and
  `Block.OutputPort` (`internal/studio/ports.go:87`) are instance methods, and
  `view.go:875` and `view.go:894` are their only callers.

## Decisions
- Add a kind-level accessor returning the schema, including each field's
  default rendered by the same `text` function the editor uses, so a default
  shown by the CLI is the value the server would store. Do not add a second
  formatting path.
- `Block.EditorFields` is re-expressed on top of the new accessor and keeps its
  signature and output exactly; `internal/web/view.go` is not restructured in
  this task. The existing catalog tests are the regression proof.
- Bounds are published as the numbers, not as the editor's Min/Max strings.
  The CLI states a range in its own words; the browser's number input keeps
  the strings it has.
- A field whose `active` predicate depends on other parameter values is
  published with that dependency named, because the CLI must be able to say
  why a flag was rejected for a given configuration rather than silently
  ignoring it.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Every kind in `blockOrder` yields a schema whose field names match exactly
  the names `validateBlockUpdate` requires; a test walks all 29 kinds and
  asserts the sets are equal in both directions.
- Every numeric field with a `bound` publishes min and max equal to the values
  `validateBound` enforces; a test asserts a value one step outside the
  published bound is rejected by `validateBlockUpdate`.
- Published defaults round-trip: applying a kind's published defaults through
  `validateBlockUpdate` succeeds for every kind.
- Port structure is reachable per kind, with the widths and channel names a
  freshly added block of that kind would have.
- `TestBlockLibraryDefinitionsOwnDefaultsAndEditors` and the rest of
  `catalog_test.go` pass unchanged.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./internal/studio/...`
- `go vet ./...`

data.title: Serve the block library and per-kind schema as JSON
data.body:
## Goal
- Put the catalog schema on the wire, so the CLI's block help and flag parsing
  read the running server's catalog rather than the catalog the client was
  compiled against.

## Context
- Depends on the JSON envelope and on the catalog accessor. Two endpoints:
  the whole library grouped by category, and one kind's full schema including
  fields and ports.
- This is the one part of the API a client may cache within a process run and
  must not cache across runs; a server upgraded behind an old client is
  exactly the drift this endpoint exists to prevent.

## Acceptance Criteria
- The library endpoint returns every kind in `blockOrder` order with kind,
  label, category, description, tag, and whether it has inputs and outputs.
- The per-kind endpoint returns the full field schema and port structure for
  a valid kind, and a 404 `not_found` envelope for an unknown one.
- A test asserts the endpoint's kind list equals `studio.BlockLibrary()`, so a
  block added to the catalog cannot be missing from the API.
- Response is stable under repetition: two calls produce identical bytes.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./internal/web/...`

data.title: Add a subcommand per block kind with catalog-generated help
data.body:
## Goal
- Make every block in the library a real subcommand with its own flags and its
  own `--help`, generated from the served schema, so an agent discovers how to
  configure a PID by asking the PID subcommand instead of reading Go source.

## Context
- Depends on the CLI client and the block schema endpoint. This is the
  self-documenting core of the whole CLI; the rest of the block commands in
  this container build on the flag mapping it establishes.
- The shape is `processlab block add <kind> [flags]`, one subcommand per kind,
  plus `processlab block list` for the library and `processlab block help
  <kind>` for a kind's full documentation without adding anything.

## Decisions
- Flag name is the catalog parameter name with underscores replaced by
  hyphens: `initial_value` becomes `--initial-value`. The mapping is stated in
  exactly one function and is used for both generation and parsing, so it
  cannot invert wrongly.
- Because the schema arrives over HTTP, the block subcommands are discovered
  at run time. `processlab block add --help` with no server reachable exits 3
  with the same message as any other command; it does not fall back to a
  compiled-in list, because a stale list is worse than an honest failure.
- A kind's `--help` prints, per field: flag, type, default, range with unit,
  allowed values for enumerated fields, and the catalog's help text. Fields
  gated by an `active` predicate print the condition under which they apply.
- `--json` on `block add` prints the created block record; text mode prints
  the new block id alone, so `$(processlab block add ...)` composes.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `processlab block list` prints every kind grouped by category; `--json`
  prints the library record.
- `processlab block add pid --flow <id> --proportional 2.5` creates the block
  and prints its id on stdout.
- `processlab block add pid --help` lists every PID field with its bound and
  unit, and exits 0.
- An out-of-range value is refused by the server and reported with the
  catalog's own wording, exit 1, nothing on stdout.
- An unknown flag exits 2 and names the flag and the kind.
- An unknown kind exits 2 and lists the valid kinds.
- A test drives at least one kind from each category and asserts the stored
  parameters match what was passed.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./cmd/...`
- `gofmt -l cmd internal` prints nothing

data.title: Add project and flowsheet commands
data.body:
## Goal
- Let a skill create and navigate the containers its flowsheets live in, which
  every later command needs an id from.

## Context
- Depends on the CLI client. Covers `studio.CreateProject`, `RenameProject`,
  `DeleteProject`, `Register`, `CreateFlow`, `RenameFlow`, `DuplicateFlow`,
  `DeleteFlow`, `ReorderFlows`, and `Workspace`.
- `studio.Register` (`internal/studio/workspace.go:199`) already computes per-project
  flow counts and the stale-run flag; the list command shows that, not a
  re-derivation.

## Decisions
- Verbs are `list`, `show`, `create`, `rename`, `duplicate`, `delete`,
  `reorder`, under the `project` and `flow` nouns.
- `create` prints the new id on stdout and nothing else in text mode.
- Deletion is irreversible and reaches blocks, connections, events and runs
  through `ON DELETE CASCADE`. A delete that would remove a project or
  flowsheet containing work requires `--force`; without it the command reports
  what would be lost and exits 1. The domain's existing refusal to delete the
  last project or last flowsheet is surfaced as-is, not duplicated.
- `flow list` accepts an optional `--project`; with no filter it lists every
  flowsheet with its project, because a skill starting cold has neither id.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `processlab project create "Boiler"` prints an id; `project list` shows it
  with a zero flow count.
- `flow create --project <id> "Level loop"` prints an id.
- `flow list --json` includes the stale-run flag and matches `Register`.
- `flow delete <id>` on a flowsheet holding blocks exits 1 and says what it
  would remove; with `--force` it succeeds.
- Deleting the last flowsheet of a project reports the domain's refusal and
  exits 1 even with `--force`.
- `flow reorder --project <id> <flowID>...` rejects an id from another project
  with the domain's message.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./cmd/... ./internal/web/...`

data.title: Add block edit, move, delete, and duplicate commands
data.body:
## Goal
- Complete block authoring past creation, reusing the generated flag mapping so
  editing a parameter reads the same as setting it at creation.

## Context
- Depends on the block subcommands and on the project and flowsheet commands.
  Covers `studio.UpdateBlock`, `MoveBlock`, `MoveBlocks`, `DeleteBlock`,
  `DeleteBlocks`, `DuplicateBlocks`.
- `UpdateBlock` requires every defined field, not a partial set: see
  `TestValidateBlockUpdateRequiresEveryDefinedField` in `catalog_test.go`. The
  command must therefore read the block's current parameters, overlay the
  flags given, and send the complete set. That read-modify-write belongs in
  one place, not in each caller.

## Decisions
- `block set <id> --<field> <value>...` edits named fields only; unnamed fields
  keep their stored values. `--name` renames.
- `block mv`, `block rm`, `block cp` take one or more ids and use the batch
  studio operations so a multi-block change stays one transaction.
- Batch limits (`maxBlocksPerRequest`) are the domain's; the CLI reports the
  refusal rather than chunking silently, because a silently split batch is no
  longer atomic.
- `block list --flow <id>` and `block show <id>` print the stored parameters
  using the catalog's own summary, so terminal output and the GUI inspector
  agree.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `block set <id> --proportional 3` changes only that field; every other
  parameter is byte-identical afterwards.
- Editing a Sum's signs down while a wire sits on a removed port is refused
  with the domain's wording (`studio.go:210`), exit 1.
- `block rm` of two ids in one call leaves neither block if the second id is
  invalid.
- `block cp` places copies one grid step down and right with the domain's
  copy-naming, and does not copy wires.
- `block mv --flow <id> <blockID>:<x>,<y> ...` moves a selection atomically.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./cmd/... ./internal/studio/...`

data.title: Add signal wiring commands
data.body:
## Goal
- Let a skill draw and remove the connections that make a set of blocks a
  flowsheet, with port and channel references it can discover.

## Context
- Depends on the project and flowsheet commands. Covers `studio.Connect`,
  `Disconnect`, `DisconnectBlock`, and the port schema published by the
  catalog accessor.
- Wiring is where the domain refuses most: no such port, occupied input port,
  unequal widths, self-connection, cross-flowsheet endpoints. Every one of
  those messages is already written in `studio.go:478-563`; the CLI shows
  them and adds none of its own.

## Decisions
- An endpoint is `<blockID>:<port>`, with the port defaulting to 0 when
  omitted, matching the server's existing optional-port behaviour
  (`server.go:460`).
- `wire list --flow <id>` prints source, target, and both port indices with
  the block names, so the output is readable without a second lookup.
- `wire rm` accepts either a connection id or a `--block` to clear every wire
  on one block, mirroring the two studio operations rather than emulating one
  with the other.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `wire connect --flow <id> 12:0 13:0` creates the connection and prints its id.
- Connecting to an occupied input port reports the domain's message, exit 1.
- Connecting mismatched widths reports the width refusal, exit 1.
- `wire rm --block <id>` removes every wire on that block and reports the count.
- `wire list --json` includes port indices and channel widths.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./cmd/... ./internal/studio/...`

data.title: Add declarative flowsheet dump and apply
data.body:
## Goal
- Let a skill author a whole flowsheet as one document and apply it, instead of
  issuing a correct sequence of dozens of mutations and unwinding by hand when
  step nineteen fails.

## Context
- Depends on the block and wiring commands, which establish every field this
  document has to carry.
- This is the command the target skill will lean on hardest: a flowsheet is a
  graph, and building a graph through imperative calls is where an agent's
  errors compound.

## Decisions
- Block identity in the document is the block name, which is already unique
  per flowsheet and already how `DuplicateBlocks` reasons about collisions.
  Ids are emitted by `dump` for reference but ignored by `apply`.
- `apply` is a reconciliation against the named state: blocks in the document
  and not on the sheet are added, blocks on the sheet and not in the document
  are removed, and matching names are updated in place. Wires are reconciled
  the same way. This is stated in the command's help, because a document that
  silently deletes is a document that must say so.
- `apply` runs as one server-side operation so a rejected document leaves the
  flowsheet untouched. A partially applied flowsheet is the failure mode this
  task exists to remove, so it is not acceptable to loop over existing
  endpoints from the client.
- `--dry-run` prints the reconciliation it would perform and changes nothing.
- The document is the same JSON in both directions: `flow dump | flow apply`
  on an unchanged flowsheet is a no-op, and that is a test, not a claim.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `flow dump --flow <id>` emits blocks with kind, name, position, parameters,
  and wires by name and port.
- `flow apply --flow <id> < doc.json` reaches the described state from an
  empty flowsheet, from a partially matching one, and from a superset.
- A document with an invalid parameter is rejected whole: the flowsheet is
  byte-identical afterwards, exit 1, the domain's message on stderr.
- `flow dump | flow apply` reports zero changes and does not move
  `model_updated_at`, so a round trip does not mark a good run stale.
- `--dry-run` output lists additions, updates, and removals separately.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./cmd/... ./internal/web/... ./internal/studio/...`

data.title: Simulation, analysis, and results from the terminal
Add simulation run and result commands
data.body:
## Goal
- Run a flowsheet from the terminal and get its time series out in a form that
  pipes into a plotter, a diff, or an agent's own analysis without a parser.

## Context
- Depends on the CLI client and the flowsheet commands. Covers `studio.Run`
  (`internal/studio/simulate.go:34`) with `SimulationRequest{Duration,
  SampleTime}`, and the stored `Snapshot.LastRun`.
- The GUI posts these two numbers as form values (`server.go:498`) and
  re-renders the workbench. The API returns the run.

## Decisions
- Text output is the series itself: a header line of channel names, then one
  row per sample, tab separated, time first. That is the unix answer to
  "what does the CLI print for a simulation" and it composes with `awk`,
  `gnuplot`, and `column`. `--json` returns the full `Simulation` record.
- `sim run` prints the series it just produced; `sim show` prints the stored
  last run without recomputing. Two verbs because re-running a slow model to
  read a result you already have is a trap an agent falls into repeatedly.
- Staleness is not hidden: when `model_updated_at` is newer than the stored
  run, `sim show` says so on stderr and still prints the series, exit 0. The
  data is real, it is just older than the model.
- A simulation that the domain refuses (algebraic loop, missing source or
  sink, delay not aligned to the sample grid) reports that refusal verbatim.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `sim run --flow <id> --duration 20 --sample-time 0.01` prints a header and
  the sample rows; row count matches the requested grid.
- Non-numeric duration or sample time exits 2 without contacting the server.
- A flowsheet with an unsolvable algebraic loop reports the domain's message
  naming the critical channels, exit 1, nothing on stdout.
- `sim show` on a flowsheet edited since its last run prints the series and a
  staleness note on stderr.
- `sim show` with no stored run exits 1 with a message that says to run one.
- `--json` output validates against the `Simulation` record the GUI receives.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./cmd/... ./internal/web/...`

data.title: Add dynamics, frequency, and loop analysis commands
data.body:
## Goal
- Reach the three analysis intents from the terminal, including the channel
  discovery a caller needs before it can name an input and an output.

## Context
- Depends on the simulation commands. Covers `studio.RunAnalysis`
  (`internal/studio/analysis_workspace.go:83`) with `AnalysisWorkspaceRequest`,
  whose intents are `dynamics`, `frequency`, and `loop`.
- A channel reference is `block:port:channel`, already parsed by
  `parseChannelRef` (`internal/web/server.go:706`). The CLI uses that exact
  spelling so a reference copied from one surface works in the other.
- `AnalysisWorkspace` carries `Inputs` and `Outputs` as `AnalysisChannel`
  lists; that is the discovery source, not a re-derivation from the block
  catalog.

## Decisions
- `analyze channels --flow <id>` lists the selectable inputs and outputs with
  their `block:port:channel` references, because a caller that cannot see the
  references cannot form a request. This is the first thing the skill will run.
- One verb per intent: `analyze dynamics`, `analyze frequency`, `analyze loop`.
  Intent is not a flag, because the required and meaningful options differ per
  intent and a single command would have to document three shapes at once.
- `--all-channels` on frequency maps to `FrequencyAllChannels`; the domain's
  channel-axis and trace-product limits are surfaced as refusals, not clamped.
- Results are cached per flowsheet by the domain and invalidated by model
  edits. `analyze show` prints the cached workspace without recomputing, and
  marks a stale record the way `sim show` does.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `analyze channels --flow <id>` prints references that `analyze dynamics`
  accepts unmodified, for a scalar flowsheet and for a named vector one.
- `analyze dynamics --flow <id> --input <ref> --output <ref>` prints the
  diagnostics; `--json` returns the `DynamicsAnalysisRecord`.
- `analyze frequency --all-channels` on a MIMO flowsheet returns singular
  values; exceeding the domain's limit reports the domain's message, exit 1.
- A frequency request above the discrete Nyquist frequency is refused with the
  domain's wording.
- A malformed channel reference exits 2 without contacting the server.
- `analyze show` after a model edit prints the record and a staleness note.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./cmd/... ./internal/web/...`

data.title: Add results export and activity commands
data.body:
## Goal
- Get a flowsheet's complete result document and its recent history out of the
  server, so a skill can hand a whole run to something else or check what it
  just changed.

## Context
- Depends on the simulation commands. `studio.ExportResults`
  (`internal/studio/results_export.go:17`) already returns the versioned
  `ResultsExport` that the GUI downloads from
  `GET /flows/{flowID}/results.json`.
- Events are the flowsheet's activity feed, written by `touchModel`
  (`internal/studio/studio.go:629`) on every model edit.

## Decisions
- `export --flow <id>` writes the export document to stdout. It is JSON in
  both modes; there is no useful tabular rendering of a document that contains
  a simulation and three analysis records, and inventing one would be a second
  authority on what a result is.
- Reuse the existing route rather than adding a parallel export endpoint. The
  document already has a `schemaVersion`; the CLI prints it in `--json` and
  refuses a version it does not understand rather than mis-reading it.
- `log --flow <id>` prints the event feed, newest first, with `--limit`.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `export --flow <id>` output parses as `ResultsExport` and matches the
  document served to the browser byte for byte.
- Export of a flowsheet with no run still succeeds, with the simulation field
  absent and the analysis workspace present.
- `log --flow <id>` shows the message `touchModel` wrote for the most recent
  edit; a layout-only move produces no new entry, matching `touchLayout`.
- `--limit 5` returns five entries.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./cmd/... ./internal/web/...`

data.title: Control design, sweeps, identification, and nonlinear workflows
Add control role commands
data.body:
## Goal
- Let a skill declare which blocks are plant, controller, measurement, and
  analysis point, which every controller design and study workflow reads first.

## Context
- Depends on the flowsheet commands. Covers `studio.ControlRoles` and
  `AssignControlRoles` (`internal/studio/control_models.go:103`), already
  served as JSON at `GET`/`PUT /flows/{flowID}/control-roles`.
- The spec is versioned and fingerprinted; the fingerprint is what candidate
  staleness checks compare (`internal/web/controller_candidates.go:80`).
- Deleting a referenced block clears the spec atomically
  (`clearControlRoleSpecForBlocks`), so the CLI never needs to repair it.

## Decisions
- `roles show --flow <id>` prints the assignment with block names; `roles set`
  takes the role assignments as flags and replaces the spec, because the domain
  operation is a whole-spec assignment and a per-role edit command would
  pretend otherwise.
- The fingerprint is printed in `--json` output. A skill that designs a
  controller needs it to understand why an apply was later refused as stale.
- If the existing route already emits a usable JSON shape, reuse it rather
  than adding an `/api/v1` twin.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `roles set --flow <id> --plant <blockID> --controller <blockID>` stores the
  spec; `roles show` reads it back with block names resolved.
- Assigning a role to a block from another flowsheet is refused with the
  domain's message, exit 1.
- Deleting a referenced block leaves `roles show` reporting the cleared spec
  rather than a dangling id.
- `roles show --json` includes the version and fingerprint.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./cmd/... ./internal/studio/...`

data.title: Expose controller candidates over JSON with stable identifiers
data.body:
## Goal
- Give the API a candidate lifecycle a stateless client can drive, so design,
  review, apply, and undo work from a CLI without the client ever holding a
  candidate value.

## Context
- A candidate cannot cross a process boundary. `PIDDesignCandidate`,
  `StateDesignCandidate`, `RobustSynthesisCandidate`, and
  `ControllerTuningCandidate` each carry an unexported `edit` that `Apply`
  requires: see the incompleteness refusals at `pid_design.go:512`,
  `state_design.go:756`, `robust_synthesis.go:487`, and
  `controller_tuning.go:674`. Serialising a candidate and posting it back
  produces a candidate that can never be applied.
- The web package already solved this with `controllerCandidateRegistry`
  (`internal/web/controller_candidates.go:52`), keyed by opaque id, one live
  candidate per flowsheet, capacity 32, with `applying`/`undoing` guards and a
  staleness comparison over `SourceModelRevision` and the control-role
  fingerprint.
- The existing candidate routes render HTML. This task gives the same registry
  a JSON surface; it does not fork the registry.

## Decisions
- The candidate id is the API's handle. Design returns the id plus the review;
  apply and undo take the id. The client never sees `edit` and never needs to.
- The three registry conflicts (`busy`, `undo available`, `capacity`) map to
  409 with their existing messages, which is why the envelope has a `conflict`
  kind at all.
- A candidate stale against the current model revision or role fingerprint is
  refused by the domain; the API reports that refusal rather than
  regenerating, because silently redesigning a controller under an agent that
  asked to apply a specific one is the worst available behaviour.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Designing twice for one flowsheet without applying replaces the first
  candidate; the first id is then unknown, 404.
- Designing while an apply is in flight returns 409 with the busy message.
- Designing after an apply, with an undo available and an unchanged model,
  returns 409 with the undo-available message.
- Applying an id that was invalidated by a model edit returns the domain's
  staleness refusal.
- Capacity is enforced at 32 with the existing message.
- The HTML candidate routes and `controller_candidates_test.go` are unaffected.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./internal/web/...`

data.title: Add controller design and review commands
data.body:
## Goal
- Generate a controller candidate from the terminal and read its review before
  deciding anything, for all four synthesis paths.

## Context
- Depends on the JSON candidate lifecycle and the control role commands.
  Covers `DesignPIDController` (`pid_design.go:74`), `DesignStateFeedback`,
  `DesignEstimator`, `DesignObserverRegulator` (`state_design.go:114,291,423`),
  `DesignRobustController` (`robust_synthesis.go:67`), `TuneController`
  (`controller_tuning.go:130`), and the matching `Review*` operations.
- Each request type is a distinct struct with its own required fields; they do
  not reduce to a common option set and must not be flattened into one.

## Decisions
- Nouns are the synthesis families: `controller pid`, `controller state`,
  `controller robust`, `controller tune`. State design's three operations are
  its verbs: `controller state feedback`, `state estimator`, `state observer`.
- Design prints the candidate id on stdout and the review summary on stderr in
  text mode, so `$(processlab controller pid ...)` yields an id while a human
  still sees the numbers. `--json` prints id and review together on stdout.
- Tuning goals are the one genuinely list-shaped input; they are read as JSON
  from stdin when `-` is given, and as repeated flags otherwise. Eight goal
  families is past the point where flags alone stay legible.
- `controller review <id>` re-prints a candidate's review without redesigning.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `controller pid --flow <id> --type PI` prints a candidate id; `controller
  review <id>` prints its margins and step metrics.
- Designing on a flowsheet with no control roles reports the domain's message,
  exit 1.
- Each of the four families is exercised end to end in the CLI test harness.
- Conflicting tuning goals surface the domain's evidence, exit 1.
- `--json` review output matches the record the GUI renders.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./cmd/... ./internal/studio/...`

data.title: Add controller apply and undo commands
data.body:
## Goal
- Commit a reviewed candidate to the flowsheet, and take it back, with the
  conflict and staleness semantics stated rather than discovered.

## Context
- Depends on the design and review commands. Covers `ApplyPIDDesignCandidate`,
  `ApplyStateDesignCandidate`, `ApplyRobustSynthesisCandidate`,
  `ApplyTuningCandidate`, and `UndoControllerCandidate`
  (`internal/studio/candidate_apply.go:269`).
- Apply is atomic and moves `model_updated_at`, which invalidates the
  flowsheet's stored simulation and analysis records. That consequence is part
  of the command's help.

## Decisions
- `controller apply <id>` and `controller undo <id>` are one command each
  across all four families; the registry knows which family an id belongs to,
  so the caller does not have to.
- Apply prints what changed: the blocks it edited and their new parameters.
  An agent that applied a controller and cannot see what moved will read the
  whole flowsheet back, and that round trip is avoidable.
- Undo is available only for the most recent apply on an unchanged model. When
  it is not available the command says which of the two conditions failed.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Apply of a fresh candidate edits the controller block and prints the change.
- Apply of an already-applied id is refused, exit 1.
- Apply of a candidate whose flowsheet was edited in between reports the
  staleness refusal, exit 1, and the flowsheet is unchanged.
- Undo restores the prior parameters exactly; `block show` before design and
  after undo produce identical output.
- Undo after a model edit is refused and names the reason.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./cmd/... ./internal/studio/...`

data.title: Own parameter sweep model sources inside Studio
data.body:
## Goal
- Give sweeps an entry point a caller can reach with data, so the CLI can run
  one at all.

## Context
- `MaterializeParameterSweep` (`internal/studio/parameter_sweep.go:104`) takes a
  `SweepModelSource` holding two function fields, `SetParameter` and `Compile`
  (`parameter_sweep.go:36-42`). No HTTP client can supply those. There is no
  `*Studio` method that builds one, and no web route reaches sweeps at all, so
  today the capability exists and is unreachable from outside the package.
- `AnalyzeParameterSweep` (`parameter_sweep.go:153`) has the same problem in
  reverse: it needs the materialised `*controlsys.ModelArray`, which is the
  `json:"-"` field of `ParameterSweep`.

## Decisions
- Add a `*Studio` operation that takes a flowsheet, a block, a `SweepSpec`, and
  an analysis spec, and returns the analysis. It owns building the source from
  the block's catalog definition, choosing the parameter setter, compiling, and
  handing the model array to the analysis. The caller states which parameter
  over which values, and nothing else.
- The parameter named in a `SweepAxis` is a catalog parameter name, so the same
  vocabulary the block subcommands use identifies a sweep axis. Do not invent a
  second naming scheme.
- `SourceModelRevision` is filled from the flowsheet, not accepted from the
  caller, so a sweep cannot claim to be against a revision it did not read.
- Serve it under `/api/v1`; the existing limits (4 axes, 64 models, and the
  response-data cap) are the domain's and are reported as refusals.

## Acceptance Criteria
- The new operation materialises and analyses a sweep over a single block
  parameter with no closures supplied by the caller.
- A parameter name that the block's catalog definition does not define is
  refused before any model is compiled.
- Every existing limit still refuses at the same boundary; the existing
  `parameter_sweep_test.go` cases pass unchanged.
- A sweep against a flowsheet edited mid-request reports the revision it read.
- The endpoint returns the analysis with worst-case frequency and time
  summaries.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./internal/studio/... ./internal/web/...`
- `go vet ./...`

data.title: Add parameter sweep commands
data.body:
## Goal
- Sweep a block parameter and see which variant is worst, which is the fastest
  way an agent learns whether a design holds across an operating range.

## Context
- Depends on the Studio sweep operation and the CLI client. The analysis
  returns per-model frequency and time summaries plus an explicit worst case
  (`SweepFrequencyAnalysis.WorstCase`, `SweepTimeAnalysis.WorstCase`).

## Decisions
- Axes are given as `--axis <parameter>=<start>:<stop>:<count>` or an explicit
  value list, repeatable up to the domain's four. A grid an agent can state in
  one flag is a grid it can vary programmatically.
- Text output is one row per variant with its coordinates, peak gain, peak
  frequency, and peak time, with the worst case marked. `--json` returns the
  whole `ParameterSweepAnalysis`.
- The heavy response arrays are `json:"-"` in the domain type and stay out of
  the CLI. A caller wanting full responses runs the analysis commands on a
  chosen variant; the sweep's job is to find that variant.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `sweep run --flow <id> --block <id> --axis tau=0.5:2.0:4` prints four rows
  and marks the worst case.
- Two axes produce the full grid in a stable coordinate order.
- A fifth axis is refused with the domain's limit message, exit 1.
- An unknown parameter name exits 1 and lists the block's parameter names.
- `--json` output round-trips through `ParameterSweepAnalysis`.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./cmd/...`

data.title: Add model study commands
data.body:
## Goal
- Report what a flowsheet's compiled model actually is — order, poles,
  stability, channel names, delays — without running anything.

## Context
- Depends on the control role commands and the CLI client.
  `NewStateSpaceModelStudy` and `NewFRDModelStudy`
  (`internal/studio/model_study.go:44,61`) take a `*controlsys.System` or
  `*controlsys.FRD`, which only the package can produce, so like sweeps this
  capability needs a Studio-level entry point before any client can reach it.
- `BuildControlModels` (`control_models.go:142`) already compiles the role-
  tagged models for a flowsheet; that is the source a study should be built
  from rather than a second compile path.
- `ModelStudyProvenance` is fully JSON-tagged and is the whole output.

## Decisions
- `study show --flow <id>` reports the provenance of the flowsheet's compiled
  plant; `--role` selects another role-tagged model when one exists.
- `PoleIssue` and the nil-able `Stable` are reported honestly: an unknown
  stability prints as unknown, not as false.
- The entry point returns provenance only. Handing a caller a system it cannot
  use is what the closure-shaped constructors already do badly.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `study show --flow <id>` prints order, inputs, outputs, sample time, and
  stability for a compiled flowsheet.
- A flowsheet whose model is an FRD reports the FRD provenance including its
  frequency sample count.
- A flowsheet that does not compile reports the compiler's refusal, exit 1.
- A model with a pole computation issue prints `PoleIssue` rather than
  omitting stability silently.
- `--json` matches `ModelStudyProvenance`.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./cmd/... ./internal/studio/...`

data.title: Add system identification commands
data.body:
## Goal
- Estimate a model from measured data supplied on stdin, so a skill can turn a
  logged experiment into a block without a GUI import step.

## Context
- Depends on the CLI client. `NewIdentificationWorkflow`
  (`internal/studio/identification_workflow.go:30`) and its methods take an
  `IdentificationDataset` that is already fully JSON-tagged, including split,
  preprocessing, sample time, and channel names and units.
- Nothing in `internal/web` reaches identification today, so this task adds
  both the endpoint and the command.

## Decisions
- The dataset arrives on stdin: JSON as the canonical form, and CSV with a
  header row as a convenience, because measured data is what people already
  have in files. CSV maps columns to input and output channels by flags naming
  them; the mapping is stated once.
- Preprocessing and the training/validation split are flags with the domain's
  own vocabulary (`none`, `remove_mean`, `linear_detrend`).
- The estimate is reported with its validation fit. An identification command
  that prints a model without saying how well it matched held-out data invites
  an agent to trust it.
- Writing the result into a flowsheet block is deliberately not in this task;
  it is a separate decision about which block and is better made once the
  estimate can be inspected.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `ident estimate --sample-time 0.1 < data.json` prints the estimated model
  and its validation fit.
- CSV input with named columns produces the same estimate as the equivalent
  JSON.
- The channel, sample, FFT, Markov, and ERA-order limits are reported as
  refusals, exit 1.
- A dataset whose split ranges overlap or exceed the sample count is refused.
- `--json` returns the full estimation record.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./cmd/... ./internal/studio/...`

data.title: Add nonlinear definition, linearization, and EKF commands
data.body:
## Goal
- Reach the nonlinear workflows from the terminal: register a definition,
  linearize it at an operating point, and run an extended Kalman filter.

## Context
- Depends on the CLI client. Covers `RegisterNonlinearDefinition`,
  `NonlinearDefinition`, `LinearizeNonlinear`, and `RunNonlinearEKF`
  (`internal/studio/nonlinear_workflow.go:157,189,227,324`).
- `RegisterNonlinearDefinition` takes `NonlinearRuntimeCallbacks` alongside the
  definition. Determine, before designing the command, which of those callbacks
  a stored definition can supply on its own and which require in-process Go
  code. Anything that cannot be expressed as data is out of the CLI's reach and
  the command must say so rather than pretend.

## Decisions
- Definitions are registered from a JSON document on stdin, matching how the
  domain already persists them.
- `nonlinear linearize` prints the linearization candidate's provenance and
  operating point; `nonlinear ekf` prints the run.
- If registration turns out to need a Go callback that no document can carry,
  this task registers only the definitions that are fully data-expressible and
  reports the others as unsupported from the CLI, naming why. That limitation
  goes in the CLI reference, not in a silent omission.

## Checkpoint
- Produce: a short note in the task's completion message stating which
  `NonlinearRuntimeCallbacks` members are data-expressible and which are not.
- Then ask: whether the non-expressible workflows should be dropped from the
  CLI, or whether the domain should gain a data-driven definition form.
- Do not proceed past registration without approval.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `nonlinear register < definition.json` stores a definition and prints its
  reference.
- `nonlinear linearize --definition <ref> --operating-point <name>` prints the
  linearization.
- `nonlinear ekf --definition <ref>` runs and prints the estimate series.
- An unnamed operating point or estimator is refused with the domain's message.
- Any workflow excluded by the checkpoint's finding is documented and exits 2
  with an explanation rather than failing obscurely.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./cmd/... ./internal/studio/...`

data.title: CLI documentation, skill, and release verification
Write the CLI reference and update the README
data.body:
## Goal
- Document the CLI where the rest of this repository documents itself, and
  make the parts that are generated stay generated.

## Context
- Depends on the command surface being complete. `README.md` has "Run it",
  "Run with Docker Compose", "Project structure", and "Validate it" sections
  that all describe a binary that only serves; every one of them changes.
- `docs/` holds one note per capability. The CLI reference belongs there as
  `docs/cli.md`, referenced from the README rather than duplicated into it.

## Decisions
- The reference states the contract a skill depends on: exit codes, stream
  discipline, the `--json` guarantee, the `PROCESSLAB_ADDR` and `--server`
  resolution order, and the fact that the CLI requires a running server and
  never opens the database.
- The per-command and per-block detail is not transcribed. It is generated
  from `processlab help --json` and the block schema endpoint by a small
  command in the repository, and the check that it is current is a test, not a
  habit. A hand-maintained flag table is exactly the second authority the
  catalog task removed.
- Record the store contract that produced the client/server split, citing
  `internal/studio/store.go:101`, so the next person to propose a `--db` flag
  on a client command finds the reason it is absent.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `docs/cli.md` exists and covers every top-level command with a worked
  example.
- The README's run, structure, and validate sections describe `processlab
  serve` and the client commands.
- A test regenerates the generated sections and fails if the committed file
  differs.
- Every example in `docs/cli.md` is executed by the CLI test harness; no
  example is aspirational.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./...`
- `npm run test:browser`

data.title: Author the flowsheet-building skill that drives the CLI
data.body:
## Goal
- Deliver the thing the CLI was built for: a skill that builds flowsheets,
  runs simulations, and prototypes control from the terminal.

## Context
- Depends on the CLI reference. The skill is a consumer, not a second
  documentation source: it tells an agent how to approach a control problem
  with this tool and points at `processlab help --json` and `processlab block
  help <kind>` for the details, which stay current on their own.
- Read `docs/control-model-roles.md`, `docs/pid-design.md`,
  `docs/loop-sensitivity.md`, and `docs/controller-candidate-workflow.md`
  before writing it. The domain sequence those describe — assign roles, build
  models, design, review, apply — is the sequence the skill must teach.

## Decisions
- The skill carries workflow and judgment: when to sweep rather than tune,
  what a stale record means, why an apply was refused, how to read a review
  before applying. It does not carry a flag reference.
- It leads with `flow dump` and `flow apply`, because building a graph
  declaratively is what keeps an agent's errors from compounding.
- It states plainly that a human may be in the GUI on the same server, so
  destructive commands are used deliberately and `--force` is not reflexive.

## Acceptance Criteria
- The skill builds a working closed-loop flowsheet from an empty project,
  simulates it, analyses the loop, designs and applies a PID, and verifies the
  improvement, using only documented commands.
- That run is reproduced end to end as a test against a throwaway server.
- The skill contains no flag table and no block parameter list.
- Following it produces no command that exits 2, because a usage error means
  the skill taught the wrong invocation.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./cmd/...`

data.title: Verify the CLI end to end and close the compatibility paths
data.body:
## Goal
- Confirm the whole surface works together and leave no half-migrated launcher
  or duplicated source of truth behind.

## Context
- Depends on the documentation. This is the sweep that catches what per-task
  gates cannot: that the Docker image, compose file, browser suite, README,
  and skill all agree about how the binary is invoked.
- The dispatcher change breaks every existing launcher. Each was updated in
  its own task; this task proves they were.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `go build ./cmd/processlab` then the binary's `serve` runs the GUI and the
  browser suite passes against it.
- `docker compose up` serves the application; the image's entrypoint uses the
  subcommand form.
- A grep for the old bare-invocation form finds no live reference in
  `README.md`, `Dockerfile`, `compose.yaml`, `browser/`, or `docs/`.
- No block parameter name, bound, unit, or help string appears in
  `cmd/processlab` or in `docs/cli.md` outside generated sections.
- The full validation set passes from a clean checkout.

## Validation Gates
- `gofmt -l cmd internal` prints nothing
- `go vet ./...`
- `go test -race ./...`
- `go build ./cmd/processlab`
- `npm install && npm run test:browser`
- `docker compose up --build` serves and shuts down cleanly

## Scope
- The `processlab` binary becomes a subcommand dispatcher and gains a JSON
  client transport. Everything the later containers add plugs into the argv,
  stream, exit-code, and error contract established here.

## Decisions that bind every container
- **Transport.** The CLI is an HTTP client of a running Process Lab server. It
  never opens SQLite. `internal/studio/store.go:101` pins the database to one
  connection and states that a second process opening the file is the point at
  which a local file stops being the right store; a direct-database client
  would put an agent and a human on opposite sides of that line. One process
  owns the data, so a flowsheet the CLI edits is the flowsheet the GUI shows.
- **One binary.** `processlab serve` starts the server with the flags it has
  today. Bare `processlab` prints help. This breaks every existing launcher;
  each is updated in the task that owns it and proved in the final container.
- **Output.** stdout carries data, stderr carries diagnostics. Text is the
  default and is line-oriented and greppable; `--json` emits the studio record
  itself. Colour and alignment only on a terminal with `NO_COLOR` unset.
- **Exit codes.** 0 success, 1 the operation was rejected or failed, 2 usage
  error, 3 no server reachable. A skill branches on these.
- **API.** `/api/v1`, JSON in and out, one error envelope with a `kind` of
  `usage`, `not_found`, `conflict`, or `internal`. It binds where `serve`
  binds, loopback by default, and adds no authentication: same trust boundary
  as the GUI it sits beside.
- **No second authority.** The CLI restates no domain rule. Bounds, defaults,
  units, help text, refusal wording, and batch limits are read from the
  catalog and the domain and passed through verbatim.

## Non-goals
- No authentication, no remote or multi-user access, no daemon management.
- No CLI framework dependency; the command tree is a Go value so it can be
  served as machine-readable help.
- No offline or `--db` mode on any client command.

## Scope
- Everything needed to build a flowsheet from nothing: the catalog as a
  published schema, a subcommand per block kind whose help is generated from
  it, project and flowsheet lifecycle, block editing, wiring, and a
  declarative dump and apply for whole sheets.

## Decisions
- The catalog is the one authority for block parameter names, types, bounds,
  units, options, defaults, and help. The CLI generates its flags and its help
  from it over HTTP, so a server upgraded behind an older client documents
  itself correctly rather than plausibly.
- Flag name is the catalog parameter name with underscores replaced by
  hyphens, mapped in one function used for both generation and parsing.
- Nouns are `block`, `project`, `flow`, `wire`; verbs follow them.
- Deleting a container that holds work requires `--force`. The domain refusals
  it already has (last project, last flowsheet) are surfaced, never restated.
- `flow dump` and `flow apply` reconcile against block names and run as one
  server-side operation, because a half-applied flowsheet is the failure this
  container exists to prevent.

## Non-goals
- No subsystem or hierarchy authoring; `docs/subsystem-design.md` is a
  separate capability that does not exist in the domain yet.
- No layout intelligence. Positions are passed through, not computed.

## Scope
- Running a flowsheet and getting results out: simulation, the three analysis
  intents with the channel discovery they need, the versioned results export,
  and the activity log.

## Decisions
- A simulation prints its time series as tab-separated columns with a header,
  so it pipes into a plotter or `awk` without a parser. `--json` gives the
  full record.
- Recompute and read-back are separate verbs (`run` versus `show`), because
  re-running a slow model to read a result already stored is a trap.
- Staleness is reported on stderr and never suppresses the data.
- Channel references keep the `block:port:channel` spelling the server already
  parses, so a reference works unchanged across both surfaces.
- The results export reuses the existing route and its `schemaVersion`; the
  CLI refuses a version it does not understand rather than misreading it.

## Scope
- The control engineering the CLI exists for: role assignment, all four
  controller synthesis families with review, apply, and undo, parameter
  sweeps, model studies, system identification, and the nonlinear workflows.

## Constraints discovered while planning
- **Candidates cannot leave the process.** `PIDDesignCandidate`,
  `StateDesignCandidate`, `RobustSynthesisCandidate`, and
  `ControllerTuningCandidate` each hold an unexported `edit` that `Apply`
  requires; a serialised candidate can never be applied. The CLI therefore
  works in candidate ids against the server-side registry that
  `internal/web/controller_candidates.go` already maintains.
- **Sweeps and studies have no reachable entry point.** `SweepModelSource`
  holds `SetParameter` and `Compile` closures, and the model study
  constructors need a `*controlsys.System`. No HTTP client can supply either,
  and no route reaches them today. Both need a `*Studio` operation that owns
  the assembly before any transport can exist, which is why those tasks come
  before their commands rather than beside them.
- Identification and the nonlinear workflows have no web surface at all, so
  each of those tasks adds both an endpoint and a command.

## Decisions
- A sweep axis names a catalog parameter, the same vocabulary the block
  subcommands use. No second naming scheme for the same thing.
- Staleness refusals are reported, never worked around. Silently regenerating
  a controller under an agent that asked to apply a specific one is the worst
  available behaviour.
- Design prints the candidate id on stdout and the review on stderr, so a
  command substitution yields an id while a human still sees the numbers.

## Open question, checkpointed
- Whether `NonlinearRuntimeCallbacks` can be expressed as data at all decides
  how much of the nonlinear workflow the CLI can reach. That task carries a
  checkpoint rather than a guess.

## Scope
- The reference, the skill that consumes it, and the sweep that proves every
  launcher moved with the binary.

## Decisions
- Per-command and per-block detail in the reference is generated from
  `processlab help --json` and the block schema endpoint, and a test fails if
  the committed file is stale. A hand-maintained flag table would be exactly
  the second authority this plan spends its first tasks removing.
- The skill carries workflow and judgment, not a flag reference: when to sweep
  rather than tune, what a stale record means, why an apply was refused. It
  points at the CLI for the details, which stay current on their own.
- The reference records why no client command has a `--db` flag, citing
  `internal/studio/store.go:101`, so the constraint outlives this plan.

data.title: Represent nonlinear models as data
data.body:
## Goal
- Make a persisted `NonlinearDefinition` executable on its own, so a nonlinear
  model is data rather than a set of Go closures registered into a process.
  This is what puts linearization and EKF within reach of any client, and it
  removes the process-local registry that exists only to hold functions.

## Context
- `internal/studio/nonlinear_workflow.go` today requires six callbacks
  (`NonlinearRuntimeCallbacks`, line 42) at registration. Only two are
  independent knowledge:
  - `Dynamics` f(x,u) and `Output` h(x,u) are irreducible.
  - `Transition` is f integrated over a sample time.
  - `Measurement` is h with the input held.
  - `TransitionJacobian` and `MeasurementJacobian` are central differences of
    those two. `controlsys` already computes Jacobians this way in
    `finiteDifferenceLocalModel` (`local_approx.go:60`), and the provenance
    string at `nonlinear_workflow.go:317` already says so. Requiring callers to
    supply them is duplicated knowledge, not a capability.
- The only callers of `RegisterNonlinearDefinition`, `LinearizeNonlinear`, and
  `RunNonlinearEKF` are in `internal/studio/nonlinear_workflow_test.go`. There
  is no route in `internal/web` and no other consumer in the repository, so the
  registration signature can change outright. Do not add a compatibility
  wrapper for a caller that does not exist.
- `docs/nonlinear-workflows.md` documents the current limitation: "Callbacks
  are process-local and must be registered again after a process restart." That
  sentence is what this task deletes. Update the document in this task.
- The flowsheet compiler stays LTI. This task does not make blocks nonlinear
  and does not let a nonlinear definition enter a flowsheet, matching the
  existing doc's first paragraph.

## Decisions
- `NonlinearDefinition` gains an expression for each state derivative and each
  output, over the declared state and input names. Definition plus expressions
  is complete: nothing else is needed to linearize or filter.
- `RegisterNonlinearDefinition` loses its `callbacks` parameter entirely. One
  way to define a nonlinear model, not two. Rewrite the package tests onto
  expressions; several of their cases (a callback returning nil, or the wrong
  length) become unreachable states rather than tested errors.
- Delete `nonlinearRuntimeDefinitions` (line 57, a package-level global shared
  by every `Studio` in the process), `nonlinearRuntimeEntry`, the
  `reflect.DeepEqual` drift check at line 607, and the error at line 602,
  "persisted but its runtime callbacks are not registered". A persisted
  definition becomes complete by construction, so that failure cannot occur.
  `NonlinearModelProvenance.RuntimeRegisteredAt` becomes the definition's
  stored creation time; keep the field, change what feeds it.
- Parse with `go/parser.ParseExpr` and walk the AST against a whitelist. No new
  dependency. Permit only: numeric literals, declared signal identifiers,
  parentheses, unary `-` and `+`, the binary operators `+ - * /`, and calls to
  a fixed function set (`sin cos tan asin acos atan atan2 sinh cosh tanh exp
  log log10 sqrt abs pow min max`). Reject every other node kind — selectors,
  indexing, assignment, strings, imaginary literals, and any statement — naming
  what was found.
- Reject `^` explicitly with a message directing the author to `pow(x, 2)`.
  Go parses `^` as bitwise XOR, so accepting it would silently compute
  something other than a power. This is the trap most likely to produce a wrong
  model that still runs.
- Identifiers resolve only to declared state and input names. An unknown
  identifier is refused naming it and listing what is declared. Refuse a
  definition that declares a signal named `pi` or `e`, so an identifier never
  has two meanings.
- Signal names in an expression-backed definition must be valid Go identifiers.
  `normalizedSignalNames` currently accepts any non-empty trimmed string,
  including names with spaces, which cannot appear in an expression. Tighten it
  and give the refusal a message that shows the offending name.
- `sampleTime` is optional on the definition and required only by the EKF,
  because linearization needs the continuous dynamics alone. `RunNonlinearEKF`
  refuses a definition without one, naming the field. `Transition` is fixed-step
  RK4 over the sample time, with an optional `integrationSteps` defaulting to 1
  for a caller who needs accuracy the measurement rate cannot give.
- An output whose expression references an input variable has direct
  feedthrough and cannot serve as an EKF measurement. This is a syntactic check
  on the parsed tree, refused at registration naming the output and the input it
  references, rather than a silent convention about which input value is held
  during an update. Linearization is unaffected; feedthrough is legitimate there
  and lands in `D`.
- Bump `nonlinearDefinitionSchemaVersion` and refuse an older stored row with
  the existing unsupported-version message. There are no deployed definitions
  to migrate; the version exists so a stale row fails loudly.
- Evaluation is bounded by an expression depth limit checked at parse time. A
  division by zero yields a non-finite value, which the existing
  `checkedVector` and `validateFiniteVector` paths already refuse with the
  callback's name, so no new failure vocabulary is needed.

## Acceptance Criteria
- A definition carrying only metadata, state and output expressions, and a
  sample time registers, survives a `Studio` reopened against the same database
  file, and linearizes and runs an EKF with no second registration step. Prove
  the restart case explicitly; it is the property the whole task exists for.
- The pendulum in the existing tests, expressed as data, linearizes to the same
  `A`, `B`, `C`, `D` as the current callback form, within finite-difference
  tolerance.
- Derived `TransitionJacobian` and `MeasurementJacobian` match analytic
  Jacobians for a model whose derivatives are known in closed form.
- `x^2` is refused with a message naming `pow`. An unknown identifier, a
  non-identifier signal name, a call to an unlisted function, and a declared
  signal named `e` are each refused with the offending text in the message.
- An output referencing an input is accepted for linearization and refused as
  an EKF measurement, naming both the output and the input.
- `RunNonlinearEKF` on a definition with no sample time is refused naming the
  field.
- No package-level mutable registry remains in the file, and two `Studio`
  instances in one process against different databases do not observe each
  other's definitions.
- `docs/nonlinear-workflows.md` describes the data form, and its
  process-local-callbacks paragraph is gone.

## Validation Gates
- `gofmt -l internal` prints nothing
- `go vet ./...`
- `go test -race ./internal/studio/...`

## Goal
- Reach the nonlinear workflows from the terminal: register a definition,
  linearize it at an operating point, and run an extended Kalman filter.

## Context
- Depends on the CLI client and on `EWVJ2D`, which makes a nonlinear
  definition self-sufficient data. That task resolved this one's original
  checkpoint: all six `NonlinearRuntimeCallbacks` members were Go function
  values and none were serialisable, so the definition form changed rather than
  the workflow being dropped. By the time this task starts, a registered
  definition carries its own dynamics and output expressions and needs no
  in-process registration.
- Covers `RegisterNonlinearDefinition`, `NonlinearDefinition`,
  `LinearizeNonlinear`, and `RunNonlinearEKF`
  (`internal/studio/nonlinear_workflow.go`). None of them has a web route
  today, so this task adds the `/api/v1` endpoints as well as the commands.
- Read `docs/nonlinear-workflows.md` first, as `EWVJ2D` leaves it. It states
  what the workflow deliberately does not do: a nonlinear definition never
  becomes a block, and linearization is candidate-only with no apply.

## Decisions
- Definitions are registered from a JSON document on stdin, matching how the
  domain persists them. `nonlinear register` prints the resulting `key@version`
  reference on stdout so a command substitution yields something usable.
- A definition is immutable at a version. The domain refuses a changed
  definition under an existing key and version; the command reports that
  refusal verbatim, including its instruction to increment the version.
- `nonlinear linearize` prints the operating point, the equilibrium residual
  norm, and the directional validity evidence, because a linearization without
  its validity radius invites a caller to trust it outside the region where it
  holds. `--json` returns the full `NonlinearLinearizationCandidate`, whose
  `System` field is `json:"-"` and therefore absent; print the state, input,
  and output names so the caller can still see the model's shape.
- `nonlinear ekf` takes its input and measurement rows on stdin as TSV, the
  same shape `sim run` writes to stdout, so a simulated run can feed a filter
  without a format conversion. Text output is the state estimate series in that
  same tabular form; `--json` returns the full `NonlinearEKFRun` with the
  per-step covariances.
- The domain's refusals are surfaced verbatim rather than pre-checked in the
  CLI: a non-equilibrium operating point, a non-symmetric or non-PSD
  covariance, a mismatched input and measurement count, and a batch over
  10,000 steps all already carry precise messages.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `nonlinear register < definition.json` stores a definition and prints its
  `key@version` reference.
- A definition registered against one server process is linearized by a later
  command against a restarted server, with no re-registration.
- `nonlinear linearize --definition <ref> --operating-point <file>` prints the
  equilibrium norm and one validity row per requested direction.
- An operating point that is not an equilibrium is refused with the domain's
  message naming the residual norm and the tolerance, exit 1.
- `nonlinear ekf --definition <ref>` reads TSV rows on stdin and prints the
  estimate series; a mismatched input and measurement count is refused with the
  domain's message, exit 1.
- A definition whose expressions are malformed reports the parse refusal from
  `EWVJ2D` naming the offending text, exit 1.
- Malformed stdin, a missing `--definition`, or an unparsable TSV row exits 2
  without contacting the server.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./cmd/... ./internal/web/... ./internal/studio/...`

data.text: Checkpoint resolved: nonlinear models become data. All six NonlinearRuntimeCallbacks were Go function values, but only Dynamics and Output are independent knowledge; Transition, Measurement, and both Jacobians derive from them. Rather than drop the workflows, EWVJ2D adds an expression-based definition form and deletes the process-global callback registry. This task now depends on EWVJ2D and its checkpoint is removed.
