data.title: PR 12 review: CLI self-documentation and correctness
Let the dispatcher own subcommand dispatch, help, and usage
data.body:
## Goal
- Make every command in the tree discoverable and self-documenting, which is
  the property the CLI was built for and currently does not have below the top
  level.

## Context
- `cmd/processlab/main.go` defines `command.children`, but no parent command
  ever populates it. `newFlowCommand`, `newBlockCommand`, `newSimulationCommand`
  and the rest hand-dispatch inside their own `run`, each building its own
  `flag.FlagSet`. The consequences are all one root cause:
  - `processlab flow --help` prints a summary and nothing else: no
    subcommands, no flags.
  - `processlab help --json` reports 15 top-level commands and `"commands":[]`
    for every one of them. That is the agent skill's discovery mechanism, so
    the skill cannot learn that `flow create` or `sim run` exist.
  - `flag.ErrHelp` is handled at 28 call sites and missed at 12, so
    `processlab flow create --help` prints `flag: help requested` and exits 2.
    The full list: `project show|create|rename|delete`,
    `flow show|create|rename|duplicate|delete|reorder`, `wire connect|rm`.
  - `controller state --help` fails differently, with
    `unknown operation "--help"`, because the dispatcher has no concept of a
    third level and `controller state feedback|estimator|observer` is one.
- Task 524F2N set the contract this breaks: "Help is never an error when asked
  for explicitly", and "A command body never calls `os.Exit`, never writes
  usage text". Task G6I4JK required that a command added later appears in the
  JSON with no edit to the help code.
- `TestRunJSONHelpIncludesEveryCommand` in `cmd/processlab/main_test.go` does
  not catch this. It walks the tree but asserts only that the root has 15
  children, and the tree is empty one level down, so it passes.
- `command.execute` has a second, separate gap: its required-argument check
  iterates `c.arguments[:set.NArg()]`, so an argument that is missing entirely
  is never reported. Only a present-but-empty argument is caught.

## Decisions
- Parents declare `children`; `execute` owns argv splitting, `--help` at every
  level, unknown-subcommand errors, and required-argument checks. Delete the
  28 duplicated `errors.Is(err, flag.ErrHelp)` blocks rather than adding 12
  more. If a subcommand still needs to write its own usage line, the
  restructure is incomplete.
- Subcommand flags move into their command's `flags` slice with the
  `register` function that already exists on `commandFlag`, so text help,
  JSON help, and actual parsing all read one declaration.
- `printCommandHelp` lists a command's children and its positional arguments.
  It currently prints neither, which is why parent help is nearly empty.
- The block kind subcommands stay generated at run time from the server's
  schema, as they are today. They are children discovered from the catalog,
  not hand-written entries, and `block help <kind>` keeps working unchanged.
- Three levels is the depth the tree actually needs (`controller state
  feedback`). Make `execute` recurse rather than special-casing a third level.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Every leaf command's `--help` exits 0, writes to stdout, and lists its flags
  with types and defaults. Prove it with a test that walks the tree and runs
  `--help` on every leaf, rather than a list of hand-written cases.
- `processlab flow --help` and `processlab controller state --help` list their
  subcommands.
- `processlab help --json` returns a non-empty `commands` array for every
  parent, and the walking test asserts every node has a non-empty summary and
  that every leaf has at least one documented flag or argument.
- The text and JSON agreement test compares the whole tree, not the root.
- A missing required positional argument exits 2 naming the argument.
- `processlab flow create --project 1 name` and every other command that works
  today still works, with the same flags and output. The restructure changes
  discovery, not behaviour.

## Validation Gates
- `gofmt -l cmd internal` prints nothing
- `go vet ./...`
- `go test -race ./cmd/...`

data.title: Make parameter activation one data-owned fact
data.body:
## Goal
- Let the catalog state once when a parameter applies, so generated help can
  say which value activates a field instead of only that something does.

## Context
- `internal/studio/catalog.go` added `activeWhen []string` beside the existing
  `active func(Parameters) bool`. The same fact is now stated twice, by hand:

      []string{"delay_mode", "sample_time_mode"},
      func(parameters Parameters) bool {
          return normalizedDelayMode(parameters) == delayModeThiran &&
              normalizedSampleTimeMode(parameters) == sampleTimeExplicit
      },

  A closure's dependencies cannot be introspected, so nothing keeps the list
  in sync with the predicate and no test can detect drift. Task ZGARBN existed
  to remove exactly this kind of second authority.
- The list carries names but not values, so help can only report that a
  dependency exists. Via the shared `sampleTimeFields()` this reaches 11 kinds
  — `pid`, `pid2`, `state_space`, `zpk`, `frd`, `mimo_transfer`, `delay`,
  `unit_delay`, `discrete_state_space`, `discrete_transfer`,
  `discretized_transfer` — all rendering:

      --sample-time   applies when --time-domain is active

  and for `delay`, `applies when --delay-mode and --sample-time-mode is
  active`, which is also ungrammatical.
- Separately, `printBlockSchemaHelp` (`cmd/processlab/block_command.go:356`)
  prints `field.Unit` inside the `Minimum != nil || Maximum != nil` branch, so
  a parameter with a unit and no bounds renders without its unit.
  `integrator.initial_condition` and `delay.initial_output` both do.

## Decisions
- The condition becomes data: a dependency name plus the values that activate
  the field. `active` is derived from that data rather than written beside it,
  so the predicate the editor evaluates and the condition help prints are the
  same fact. A field whose activation genuinely cannot be expressed this way
  keeps a closure, but then it publishes no condition at all rather than a
  misleading one.
- Help renders the value: `applies when --time-domain is discrete`, and joins
  multiple conditions with `and`.
- The block help printer renders every attribute the schema publishes. Unit is
  printed whenever it is present, independently of bounds.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `processlab block help pid` prints `applies when --time-domain is discrete`,
  and `block help delay` names both conditions with their values.
- `processlab block help integrator` prints the unit for
  `--initial-condition`.
- A test asserts the single-authority property directly: for every kind and
  every parameter that publishes a condition, setting the dependency to each
  of its option values makes the derived `active` predicate agree with the
  published condition. A hand-maintained name list cannot satisfy this test.
- No `[]string` of dependency names remains in `catalog.go`.
- The workbench editor shows and hides conditional fields exactly as it does
  today; `internal/web` template tests pass untouched.

## Validation Gates
- `gofmt -l cmd internal` prints nothing
- `go test -race ./internal/studio/... ./internal/web/... ./cmd/...`
- `npm run test:browser`

data.title: Report routing and transport failures honestly
data.body:
## Goal
- Stop a mistyped URL from reading as a deleted record, and stop a proxy
  failure from reading as a usage error, so a client can act on what it is
  told.

## Context
- `internal/web/server.go:46` registers the `/api/v1` fallback as a handler
  returning `studio.ErrNotFound`. Every unrouted path therefore answers
  `{"error":{"kind":"not_found","message":"The requested item no longer
  exists."}}`. A path typo and a deleted flowsheet are indistinguishable,
  which is a bad trap for a client that builds paths programmatically.
- `cmd/processlab/client.go:140` assigns `kind: "usage"` whenever a >=400
  response body is not a valid envelope. An upstream proxy's HTML 502 or a bare
  `404 page not found` from a non-API route is then labelled a usage error.
  During review a stray process on the default port produced exactly this.

## Decisions
- The API fallback keeps kind `not_found` — the status is right — but carries
  its own message naming the method and path that matched no route. Route
  misses and record misses are different failures and say so.
- A response the client cannot decode as an envelope is kind `internal`, not
  `usage`. The exit code stays 1; only the vocabulary changes.
- The client's fallback message keeps the response body when it is short and
  plainly text, because it is often the only diagnostic available, but it
  never presents it as a domain message.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `GET /api/v1/nosuchroute` returns 404 with a message naming the path, and
  that message is not the missing-record wording.
- A request for a genuinely missing record still returns the record wording.
- A >=400 response with a non-JSON body surfaces kind `internal`, exit 1, with
  the body visible on stderr.
- Existing `internal/web` API tests pass untouched.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./internal/web/... ./cmd/...`

data.title: Scope the duplicate-block position exclusion and pin the placement
data.body:
## Goal
- Keep the duplicate-placement fix this branch introduced, without letting a
  duplicate land on top of the block it was copied from, and hold both
  properties with a test.

## Context
- `internal/studio/studio.go:408` passes `map[int64]bool{block.ID: true}` to
  the new `openPositionExcluding`. The fix is real: `GridPitch` is 20 and
  `BlockWidth` is 172 (`internal/studio/model.go:134`), so the desired
  position at source + one grid step always overlapped the source itself,
  `available(desired)` was always false, and every duplicate fell through to
  the reading-order lattice scan instead of landing one step down and right as
  `DuplicateBlocks`' doc comment says.
- The exclusion is too broad. It removes the source from the occupancy set for
  the whole search, including the lattice fallback, so when another block does
  occupy the down-right offset the scan can return a cell overlapping the
  original. That is a new way for two blocks to sit on top of each other.
- This is a workbench behaviour change that arrived in a CLI branch and has no
  test: `DuplicateBlocks` appears in no `_test.go` file in the repository.

## Decisions
- The source is excluded only while checking whether the desired position is
  free. The fallback scan sees every block, including the source, so no
  placement it returns can overlap anything.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Duplicating a block with clear space places the copy at exactly source plus
  one `GridPitch` in x and y.
- Duplicating a block whose down-right offset is occupied places the copy at a
  lattice position that overlaps no block, including the source.
- Duplicating every block of a full selection leaves no two blocks
  overlapping.
- The browser suite's duplicate shortcut behaves as before.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./internal/studio/...`
- `npm run test:browser`

data.title: Tighten the flowsheet document surface
data.body:
## Goal
- Make `flow dump` and `flow apply` state their own contract, since a
  declarative document is the command an agent leans on hardest and the one
  where a silent misunderstanding does the most damage.

## Context
- `flow apply` prints empty section headers on a no-op run:

      Added:
      Updated:
      Removed:
      Wires: +0 -0
      No changes.

- `flow dump` mixes two identity schemes in one document: blocks carry `id`,
  while wires reference blocks by `name`
  (`{"source":"Step 1","sourcePort":0}`). `apply` matches on name, so `id` is
  not part of the round-trip contract, and nothing says so. An agent that
  renames a block between dump and apply gets an add plus a remove rather than
  a rename, and loses that block's wires.

## Decisions
- Empty sections are not printed. A run that changed nothing prints only
  `No changes.`
- `dump` keeps `id`, because `block set`, `wire connect`, and the analysis
  channel references all take ids and a dump is the natural place to read
  them. `apply` ignores `id` and matches on name, and both the command help
  and `docs/cli.md` say so in those words.
- `apply` refuses a document containing duplicate block names, naming the
  duplicate, because name is the matching key and a duplicate silently makes
  one block unreachable.
- The rename hazard is documented where it will be read: a rename between dump
  and apply is an add and a remove, so rename with `flow rename` or
  `block set` rather than by editing a dumped document.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `flow apply` with an unchanged document prints exactly `No changes.` and
  exits 0.
- `flow apply` with changes prints only the non-empty sections.
- A document with two blocks of the same name is refused naming it, exit 1,
  with no partial application.
- `flow dump | flow apply | flow dump` remains byte-identical, as it is today.
- `processlab flow apply --help` states that `id` is ignored and that matching
  is by name.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./cmd/... ./internal/studio/... ./internal/web/...`

## Scope
- Defects found reviewing PR 12 (`codex/processlab-cli-foundation`, 22
  commits, +9880/-53) against the CLI plan. Everything here is a fix to work
  already on that branch, not new capability.

## What the review confirmed works
- Exit codes hold the contract: 0 success, 1 domain refusal, 2 usage, 3
  unreachable server, verified against a live server and a closed port.
- Stream discipline is correct; `sim run` emits the tab-separated series the
  plan specified; staleness prints the series on stdout with the warning on
  stderr and exit 0.
- `flow dump | flow apply | flow dump` is byte-identical and idempotent.
- `block help <kind>` is genuinely generated from the catalog, with real
  bounds, units, options, and defaults.
- Internal errors return "The operation could not be completed." and log the
  original, so nothing leaks. Request decoding checks content type, size, and
  that the body is exactly one JSON value.
- `gofmt`, `go vet`, and `go test ./...` all pass on the branch.

## The two findings that matter
- **The command tree is invisible below the top level.** `command.children`
  exists and is never populated; every parent hand-dispatches inside its own
  `run`. So `processlab help --json` — the discovery mechanism the agent skill
  depends on — reports zero subcommands, `flow --help` prints nothing useful,
  and 12 subcommands exit 2 on `--help` with `flag: help requested`. The CLI is
  not self-documenting below level one, which is the branch's headline claim.
- **`activeWhen` reintroduces a second authority.** A hand-written list of
  dependency names now sits beside the `active` predicate that already encodes
  the same fact, and it drops the triggering value, so 11 block kinds render
  "applies when --time-domain is active". Nothing can keep the two in sync,
  because a closure's dependencies are not introspectable. This is the exact
  duplication task ZGARBN existed to remove.

## Decisions
- Fix by deletion where possible. The dispatcher task removes 28 duplicated
  `flag.ErrHelp` blocks rather than adding the 12 that are missing; the
  activation task removes the name list rather than adding a test that cannot
  work.
- Behaviour that works today does not change. These tasks alter discovery,
  error vocabulary, and placement, not the command surface a caller uses.
- The `DuplicateBlocks` change on the branch is a genuine fix and is kept. Only
  its over-broad exclusion is narrowed, and it gains the test it never had.

## Ordering
- The dispatcher task comes before the activation task because it decides who
  renders help, and before `MWUETM` because that task generates documentation
  from `processlab help --json`, which is empty below the root until this is
  fixed.
- All five come before `2URCXX`, the final end-to-end verification sweep.

data.title: Let `nonlinear ekf` express an actual filter
data.body:
## Goal
- Make the EKF command run the filter the caller means, instead of a fixed one
  it never chose and cannot see.

## Context
- `nonlinearEKFRequest` (`cmd/processlab/nonlinear_command.go:269-297`)
  hardcodes the whole estimator:

      InitialState:      make([]float64, n),   // always zeros
      ProcessNoise:      identity(n),          // Q
      MeasurementNoise:  identity(p),          // R
      InitialCovariance: identity(n),          // P0

  and the command exposes only `--definition` and `--json`. Q and R are the
  filter: they state how far to trust the model against the sensors. Fixed at
  identity, every system gets the same gains no matter its real noise, and
  `studio.validatePSDCovariance` — which checks dimensions, symmetry, and
  positive semidefiniteness — can never fire from the CLI because identity
  always passes.
- `studio.NonlinearEKFDefinition` already carries `Name`, `InitialState`,
  `ProcessNoise`, `MeasurementNoise`, and `InitialCovariance`, all with JSON
  tags. Nothing in the domain needs to change; this is a missing input path.
- Second defect in the same command. `readNonlinearTSV`
  (`nonlinear_command.go:202`) validates that the header starts with `time`,
  has no empty columns, and repeats no name — then discards the names.
  Column-to-signal mapping is positional: `values[:m]` are inputs and the rest
  are measurements. The same numbers with the columns relabelled in the
  opposite order produce a completely different estimate, both exiting 0:

      time  torque  angle   ->  0.0667      -0.0000003
      time  angle   torque  ->  0.0000017    0.0009995

  `sim run` orders its columns by the flowsheet's scope blocks, not by the
  nonlinear definition's declared signal order, and `docs/cli.md` recommends
  piping one into the other. That pipeline silently produces wrong numbers
  whenever the two orders differ.

## Decisions
- The estimator arrives as a JSON document named by `--estimator <file>`,
  matching `nonlinear linearize --operating-point <file>`. Samples keep stdin;
  one file flag beside one stdin stream is the shape the sibling command
  already uses, and matrices do not belong on a command line.
- `--estimator` stays optional. Omitted, the command keeps today's identity Q,
  R, and P0 and zero initial state, states that on stderr in one line, and says
  so in `--help`. A quick exploratory run stays one command, but nothing
  presents a default filter as a designed one.
- TSV columns bind by name. The header must contain every declared input name
  and every declared output name; a missing one is refused naming the signal
  and listing the header. Extra columns are ignored, because `sim run` output
  legitimately carries scope channels the definition does not model — that
  tolerance is what makes the documented pipeline work.
- Positional binding is not kept as a fallback. Two mapping rules for one file
  format is how a caller gets the wrong answer without an error.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `nonlinear ekf --definition <ref> --estimator est.json < samples.tsv` uses
  the supplied Q, R, P0, initial state, and estimator name, and a run with
  different Q produces a different estimate.
- A non-symmetric or non–positive-semidefinite Q, R, or P0 is refused with the
  domain's message, exit 1.
- An estimator whose vector or matrix dimensions disagree with the definition
  is refused naming the field and both sizes.
- Omitting `--estimator` runs with identity covariances, prints one line on
  stderr saying so, and still writes only the series to stdout.
- A TSV whose columns are relabelled in a different order produces the **same**
  estimate as the original ordering. This is the regression test for the defect
  and must fail against today's code.
- A TSV missing a declared input or output column is refused naming that
  signal, exit 1.
- A TSV carrying extra columns beyond the declared signals still runs.
- `docs/cli.md` and `docs/nonlinear-workflows.md` show the estimator document
  and state that columns bind by name.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./cmd/... ./internal/studio/...`
- `go vet ./...`

data.title: Say it once and say it right in two catalog and CLI leftovers
data.body:
## Goal
- Clear the two small duplications the re-review found, while the reasons are
  still written down.

## Context
- `cmd/processlab/block_edit_command.go:151` and `:185` build their summaries
  with `fmt.Sprintf("%s %d blocks", verb, len(ids))` and
  `fmt.Sprintf("moved %d blocks", len(moves))`, so a single-block operation
  reports "duplicated 1 blocks" and "moved 1 blocks". `studio.DuplicateBlocks`
  already gets this right, producing "Duplicated 1 block", so the CLI is both
  wrong and a second author of a message the domain already writes.
- `parameterActivationValue` (`internal/studio/catalog.go:2170`) maps a
  dependency's name to its current value with a hardcoded switch over
  `delay_mode`, `sample_time_mode`, and `time_domain`, falling through to
  `default: return ""`. Every one of those cases repeats what that field's own
  `text func(Parameters) string` already computes — `sample_time_mode`'s case
  is character-for-character its `text` body. The comment at `catalog.go:124`
  states the rule this breaks: "Nothing outside the definition switches on
  Name again."
- `TestParameterActivationDataDrivesValidationAndSchema` does catch drift here,
  so this is not urgent and not a correctness bug. It is the duplication the
  activation work was meant to end, left one level down.

## Decisions
- The CLI reports what the server reported. Where the domain already composes a
  summary, print it rather than recomposing it; where the CLI must build one,
  it agrees with the count.
- `parameterActivationValue` resolves the dependency's `parameterDefinition`
  and calls its `text`, so a field's value has one reader. The silent `""`
  default goes with it: an activation naming a parameter that does not exist is
  a programming error the catalog should refuse loudly, not a condition that
  quietly never matches.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `block cp` on one block reports "1 block"; on several, "N blocks". Same for
  `block mv` and `block rm`.
- No `switch` over parameter names remains in `catalog.go`.
- An activation naming an undeclared parameter fails loudly — a test asserts
  it, rather than the field silently never activating.
- `TestParameterActivationDataDrivesValidationAndSchema` passes unchanged; it
  is the proof the refactor preserved behaviour.
- Block help output for every kind is byte-identical before and after.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./internal/studio/... ./cmd/...`
- `gofmt -l cmd internal` prints nothing

## Scope
- Second review pass over `codex/processlab-cli-foundation`, after the five
  fixes in container `EJZY6J` landed. Three findings, all new.

## What this pass confirmed fixed
- Every subcommand's `--help` exits 0, including the third level
  (`controller state feedback`) and the new `nonlinear` commands. `help --json`
  returns a fully populated tree. The dispatcher refactor was a net deletion of
  91 lines across 17 files.
- Activation is data-owned: `active` is derived from `activation`, help reads
  `applies when --time-domain is discrete`, and delay names both conditions
  with their values. Units print without bounds.
- Unrouted API paths name the method and path; missing records keep their own
  wording; non-envelope bodies map to `internal`.
- A duplicated block lands at exactly source plus one `GridPitch`.
- `flow apply` prints only `No changes.` on a no-op, refuses duplicate block
  names, and documents that ids are ignored and matching is by name.
- The nonlinear keystone holds: a definition registered before a server restart
  linearizes after it with no re-registration. All five expression guards fire
  with precise messages, and the feedthrough rule is right in both directions.

## Findings
- **The suite is red.** `TestCLIHarnessRunsRealBinaryAndCleansUp` asserts pid
  renders a condition that belongs to `delay`. The product is correct; the
  assertion is stale. Until it lands, no other task's validation gates can be
  trusted, so it goes first and merges on its own.
- **`nonlinear ekf` cannot express an EKF.** Q, R, P0, and the initial state
  are hardcoded to identity and zeros with no way to supply them. The
  covariances are the filter, and the domain's PSD validation is unreachable
  from the CLI as a result. The `EY6Q3H` task body specified the TSV input and
  the output shape but never said how the estimator is configured, so this is a
  gap in the plan rather than a departure from it.
- **TSV header names are validated then ignored.** Binding is positional, so
  the same numbers with relabelled columns yield unrelated estimates and both
  exit 0. `docs/cli.md` recommends piping `sim run` into `nonlinear ekf`, and
  `sim run` orders columns by scope block, not by declared signal order.

## Ordering
- `SZDLXJ` first and alone: a red suite makes every other task's gates
  meaningless. `2GME23` and `7HKZ6Q` follow it and are independent of each
  other.

data.title: Green the CLI harness test and confirm nothing is masked behind it
data.body:
## Goal
- Get `go test ./...` green and keep it green, by fixing the last wrong literal
  in the CLI harness test and confirming nothing else is hidden behind it.

## Context
- `go test ./cmd/processlab/` fails on
  `TestCLIHarnessRunsRealBinaryAndCleansUp`. Reproduce with:

      go test ./cmd/processlab/ -run TestCLIHarnessRunsRealBinaryAndCleansUp

- `cmd/processlab/client_test.go:142` asserts the integrator's help contains
  `"default 0 sec"`. The integrator's `initial_condition` carries the unit
  `scalar`, so the real output is `default 0 scalar`. The product is correct;
  the literal is wrong. Change the test, not the help text.
- That literal arrived in `84ce6f7`, not in `SZDLXJ`. It was **masked**: the
  earlier assertion at line 117 aborted the test with `t.Fatalf` before line
  142 ever ran. `SZDLXJ` fixed line 117 and unmasked this one. That is the
  whole failure mode to guard against here — a `t.Fatalf` chain hides every
  assertion after the first bad one, so fixing one literal at a time and
  stopping reveals the next only on the following run.
- Two consecutive rounds of work have now been reported complete with a red
  suite, both from wrong string literals in this one file. The gate command
  exists precisely to catch this and was not run to completion.
- Cross-checking every help literal the test asserts against a live server
  leaves exactly one mismatch:

      OK       applies when --delay-mode is thiran and --sample-time-mode is explicit
      OK       applies when --time-domain is discrete
      OK       default 0 scalar
      MISSING  default 0 sec

## Decisions
- Fix the literal, then run the whole package to completion rather than the
  single test, because a `t.Fatalf` chain only reveals one failure per run.
- Add no new assertions in this task. The point is a green gate, not more
  coverage; new literals are how this file got here.
- Land this alone. Until the suite is green, no other task's validation gates
  can be trusted, which is what let the previous two rounds close on red.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `go test -race ./...` passes from a clean checkout, run to completion, with
  the output showing every package.
- No non-test file changes. If the fix appears to need product code, stop: the
  diagnosis above is wrong and the task needs re-reading.
- `TestCLIHarnessRunsRealBinaryAndCleansUp` runs past every assertion it
  contains, including the `block add pid --json` decode and the per-kind table
  after it, rather than aborting early.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./...` run to completion, all packages reported
- `go vet ./...`
- `gofmt -l cmd internal` prints nothing

data.title: Honour --help on block set and stop the schema printer naming block add
data.body:
## Goal
- Close the last hole in the CLI's self-documentation: the one command that
  still refuses `--help`, and the help line that names the wrong command.

## Context
- `processlab block set --help` exits 2 with
  `processlab block set: expected a block id`. It is the only command left that
  consumes argv without honouring `--help`, because its flags are the catalog
  parameters of whatever kind the target block happens to be, so it parses the
  id before it can know its own flags.
- This is **not** a regression from recent work. It fails identically on a
  binary built before the dispatcher refactor; it was simply missed, because
  the audit that found the other twelve did not include `block set`.
- `processlab block set <id> --help` already works and prints that block's
  catalog-generated help. Only the form with no id fails, and the fix is to
  give it the general form the way `block add --help` does — `block add` with
  no kind prints usage plus the valid kinds rather than an error.
- `printBlockSchemaHelp` (`cmd/processlab/block_command.go:370`) hardcodes
  `"Usage: processlab block add %s [flags]"`. Because `block set <id> --help`
  reuses that printer, it prints `Usage: processlab block add source [flags]`
  when the caller asked about `set` — it names a different command than the one
  being described.
- `processlab help block --json` reports `"arguments": []` for `set`, though a
  block id is required.

## Decisions
- `block set --help` with no id prints the general usage, states that the
  parameter flags come from the target block's kind, and points at
  `block set <id> --help` and `block help <kind>`. It exits 0, because help
  asked for explicitly is never an error.
- The schema help printer takes the command it is describing rather than
  assuming `add`, so one printer serves both callers without either lying.
- `block set` declares its block-id argument in the command tree so text and
  JSON help both report it as required.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `processlab block set --help` exits 0, writes to stdout, and names both
  `block set <id> --help` and `block help <kind>`.
- `processlab block set <id> --help` prints `Usage: processlab block set <id>`
  rather than `block add`, and still lists that block's parameters with their
  bounds, units, and options.
- `processlab block add <kind> --help` is byte-identical to today.
- `processlab help block --json` reports the block-id argument for `set` as
  required.
- A test walks the tree and asserts every leaf's `--help` exits 0 with empty
  stderr, so the next command with hand-rolled argv parsing cannot reopen this
  hole quietly.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./cmd/...`
- `go vet ./...`

data.title: Cover every freeform leaf in the help guard
data.body:
## Goal
- Make the leaf-help guard cover every leaf, so the next command that parses
  argv by hand cannot quietly stop honouring `--help`.

## Context
- `TestRunLeafHelp` (`cmd/processlab/main_test.go:161`) walks the command tree
  and asserts that each leaf's `--help` exits 0, writes something to stdout, and
  writes nothing to stderr. For ordinary leaves it does exactly that.
- Its `freeform` branch is gated on a single hardcoded path:

      if current.freeform {
          if strings.Join(path, " ") == "processlab block set" {
              ...assert --help...
          }
          return
      }

- There are two freeform commands: `block add` (`block_command.go:98`) and
  `block set` (`:116`). So `block add` is skipped today, and any freeform
  command added later is skipped silently by default.
- Freeform commands are the ones that consume argv themselves because their
  flags are catalog parameters rather than a fixed set. That is the exact class
  that produced the original defect: `block set --help` exited 2 for the whole
  life of the branch and no test noticed. A guard that names one command by
  string does not guard the class.
- `processlab block add --help` already exits 0 and prints usage plus the valid
  kinds, so widening the assertion should pass without any production change.

## Decisions
- The freeform branch asserts on every freeform leaf. Delete the path
  comparison rather than extending it with a second name; a list of exempt
  commands is the same defect one line later.
- No production code changes. If widening the test fails, that is a real defect
  in the command it caught — report it rather than re-narrowing the test.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `TestRunLeafHelp` contains no comparison against a specific command path.
- The test exercises `block add` and `block set`, and fails if either stops
  exiting 0 with empty stderr and non-empty stdout. Prove the guard bites by
  temporarily breaking one locally and confirming the failure, then reverting.
- `go test -race ./...` passes, run to completion with every package reported.

## Validation Gates
- `go test -race ./cmd/...`
- `go test -race ./...` run to completion
- `gofmt -l cmd internal` prints nothing

data.title: Interactive engineering plots and run comparison
data.body:
## Goal
- Make Process Lab simulation and control-analysis plots readable, inspectable, comparable, and exportable without replacing the server-rendered Go/HTMX architecture.

## Scope
- Engineering axes, grids, reference lines, and annotations for simulation, step, Bode, pole-zero, Nyquist, Nichols, singular-value, and root-locus plots.
- Pointer and keyboard inspection with synchronized cursors for plots that share a domain.
- A bounded simulation-run history, baseline comparison, difference presentation, and CSV export.
- A focused analysis dock with explicit Simulation, Dynamics, Frequency, Loop, and Compare modes.

## Non-goals
- No SPA framework, third-party charting runtime, streaming simulation, or new analysis algorithms.
- No database migration: existing simulation_runs rows already retain complete results.
- No automatic tolerance-based certification in this slice; comparison is visual and numerical.

## Decisions
- The server remains authoritative for runs, plot scales, ticks, labels, and engineering annotations. JavaScript owns only ephemeral cursor, zoom, and series-visibility state.
- Normal HTML must contain readable plots and links. HTMX swaps enhance the same canonical routes; history restore still returns a full document.
- Plot interaction reads the server-rendered SVG geometry and scale metadata instead of duplicating all samples into HTML.
- Recent-run queries are bounded and newest-first. A selected baseline is identified by stored run id and must belong to the current flowsheet.
- Comparison aligns same-identity channels by their stable block, port, and channel tuple; nonmatching channels are reported rather than silently paired.
- Existing user changes in .ergo/plans.jsonl and .local are preserved. Git staging, commits, pushes, and PR actions are outside this authorization.

## Validation
- Focused Go and JavaScript tests per task, then go test -race ./..., go vet ./..., go build ./..., npm run test:browser, formatting, and git diff --check.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Pointer movement places a crosshair at the nearest rendered vertex and reports x plus every visible series value at that domain position.
- Plots in one group synchronize the x cursor, including Bode magnitude and phase.

- Hidden series stay out of the readout.
- Initialization is idempotent across first load, repeated HTMX settle, and history restore, with no duplicate listeners.
- Reduced-motion users receive no animated cursor transition.
- Persistent Node tests cover path parsing, scale inversion including logarithmic axes, nearest-point selection, linked groups, keyboard behavior, hidden series, and repeated initialization.

data.body:
# Extend model-context sample-time propagation

## Goal
- Generalize inherited discrete sample-time resolution from Unit Delay-only forward propagation to the whole current single-rate model context, so analysis and simulation compile the same authored diagram without requiring a caller-supplied rate when a connected explicit rate is authoritative.

## Context
- MathWorks defines inherited sample time as a compile-time model-context decision and describes iterative forward and backward propagation. A Gain carries the effective rate of its signal. Unit Delay, Discrete Transfer Fcn, and Discrete State-Space accept inherited sample time. References: https://www.mathworks.com/help/simulink/ug/how-propagation-affects-inherited-sample-times.html, https://www.mathworks.com/help/simulink/ug/types-of-sample-time.html, https://www.mathworks.com/help/simulink/slref/unitdelay.html, https://uk.mathworks.com/help/simulink/slref/discretetransferfcn.html, and https://www.mathworks.com/help/simulink/slref/discretestatespace.html.
- Current authority is internal/studio/time_domain.go resolveModelSampleTimes. It knows all explicit discrete rates but only propagates forward when the target kind is Unit Delay. Catalog nil timeDomain means rate-neutral; internal/studio/catalog.go and internal/studio/rich_lti.go are the block-domain authority.
- Selected natural family: build single-rate connected regions from catalog-neutral blocks and discrete blocks. Explicit discrete blocks are anchors. Any discrete block whose catalog domain reports inherited receives the unique anchor rate reachable through neutral or inherited nodes, in either connection direction and transitively. Continuous blocks are barriers.
- Existing inherited-capable public blocks are Unit Delay, Discrete Transfer Function, Discrete State-Space, Discretized Transfer, and Thiran Transport Delay. Use catalog domain classification rather than a kind list so a future inherited discrete PID also participates without a resolver change.
- Two call shapes were evaluated. Keep the existing one-shot resolveModelSampleTimes(blocks, connections, baseStep) operation returning realized block copies plus the effective-rate map. Reject a stateful resolver or separate infer/apply calls because they add lifecycle and let callers mispair applied blocks with fidelity rates.
- resolveModelSampleTimes remains the sole policy owner. compileRequestedModel calls it once; realizations consume its compiled copies; compiledModel stores its effective-rate map; fidelity reads that map while provenance retains authored parameters.
- If a region has no explicit anchor, preserve the current positive run-step fallback. If it has multiple distinct explicit anchor rates and includes inherited blocks, return a deterministic invalid-model error naming the conflicting blocks/rates. Equal anchors are one rate. Do not silently choose a fastest or GCD rate.
- Compatibility policy: keep explicit 0.1-second new-block defaults, persisted JSON, and authored explicit/inherited modes unchanged; no migration. Only compile-time copies become explicit for realization. Existing valid explicit models and unanchored inherited simulations keep their behavior. A previously invalid analysis can now compile from model context; conflicting rates remain invalid but may receive clearer diagnostics.
- Likely files: internal/studio/time_domain.go; internal/studio/time_domain_test.go; one public analysis regression in internal/studio/analysis_frequency_test.go or internal/studio/analysis_workspace_test.go; docs/simulink-r2026a-compatibility.md. Catalog code should need no new resolver policy.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Forward propagation crosses one or more catalog-neutral blocks and works for every current discrete+inherited catalog domain, not only Unit Delay.
- Backward propagation resolves an upstream inherited discrete block from a downstream explicit discrete anchor through neutral paths.
- Propagation is transitive, independent of block and connection ordering, and accepts multiple equal-rate anchors.
- An inherited region with no explicit anchor still resolves from a positive run base step and still gives missing-base-step guidance to analysis.
- Distinct explicit rates in one inherited single-rate region fail deterministically with block and rate context; no implicit rate transition, fastest-rate heuristic, or GCD scheduling is introduced.
- Public failing regression: Studio frequency analysis with no BaseStep for Source -> explicit Discrete Transfer Function at 0.2 s -> Gain -> inherited Discrete State-Space succeeds after this change and reports Nyquist pi/0.2. Today it fails because the inherited state-space block falls back to baseStep zero. Add the reverse-direction counterpart with inherited Discrete Transfer Function -> Gain -> explicit Discrete State-Space at 0.2 s.
- Simulation fidelity reports each effective rate and authored mode; model provenance and persisted parameters remain inherited where authored.
- Update compatibility documentation to state bidirectional neutral-path propagation and retain multirate limitations.

## Non-goals
- General multirate or hybrid execution, segmented zero-order-hold scheduling, sample offsets, variable-step heuristics, fastest/GCD inference, or a Rate Transition block.
- Changing run output-grid semantics or allowing a run step that does not match the compiled single discrete rate.
- Changing catalog defaults, persistence schemas, dimension inference, PID editor fields, or controller behavior.
- Propagating through continuous-domain blocks or treating a rate conflict as a valid conversion.

## Validation Gates
- Run: GOCACHE=/private/tmp/process-lab-go-cache go test ./internal/studio -run SampleTime -count=1.
- Run: GOCACHE=/private/tmp/process-lab-go-cache go test ./internal/studio -run inherited -count=1.
- Run: GOCACHE=/private/tmp/process-lab-go-cache go test ./internal/studio -run FrequencyAnalysis -count=1.
- Run: gofmt -l on changed Go files and git diff --check.
- Deferred: repository-wide race, vet, build, HTMX, and browser gates run in task 6NBONY.

## Goal
- Let newly authored scalar-parameter Gain and Unit Delay blocks inherit one-dimensional signal width from connected model context, so a vector source can pass through shape-preserving blocks without repeated width edits while existing scalar and named-MIMO models keep their authored meaning.

## Context
- Current evidence: `Block.portSchema` in `internal/studio/ports.go` derives ports only from one block; `validateConnectionWidth` is repeated by `Studio.Connect`, `UpdateBlock` adjacency guards, `ApplyFlow`, and `compileRequestedModel`. `directSignalPortSchema` in `internal/studio/direct_vector_compatibility.go` reads `Parameters.SignalWidth`; zero normalizes to legacy scalar width one. Current public regression `TestR2026aVectorUnitDelayRunsAtInheritedRateThroughPublicStudio` must author `signal_width` before the vector wire is accepted.
- Official current behavior: Simulink computes inherited signal properties during diagram compilation and rejects inconsistent/underspecified properties: https://www.mathworks.com/help/simulink/ug/how-simulink-signals-propagate-in-a-model.html. Nonsource output dimensions generally follow inputs after supported scalar expansion: https://www.mathworks.com/help/simulink/ug/determining-output-signal-dimensions.html. Unit Delay accepts one scalar/vector input and returns the same delayed shape, with scalar/vector initial condition: https://www.mathworks.com/help/simulink/slref/unitdelay.html.
- Natural family for this slice: shape-preserving 1-D blocks with scalar parameters. Gain broadcasts scalar K over every inherited channel; Unit Delay preserves input width and broadcasts a scalar initial condition. Forward propagation may pass transitively through Gain and Unit Delay chains and fan-out. The source port or a non-scalar Unit Delay initial condition supplies a known width.
- Design considered twice. Reject a per-edge shape such as `validateConnectionWidth(source, target, allowInherited)` because callers would own propagation order, retries, and conflict policy. Choose one whole-model authority such as `resolveModelSignalWidths(blocks, connections) ([]Block, error)`: it clones authored blocks, derives effective widths to a fixed point, validates every connection against the resolved copies, and returns the copies used for port display/realization. Keep the operation unexported inside `studio`; do not add caller-managed flags or phases.
- Every complete or prospective graph must use that authority: `compileRequestedModel`; `Studio.Connect` after adding the candidate wire; `Studio.UpdateBlock` after replacing the candidate block; `ApplyFlow` after preparing all desired blocks/wires; and snapshot/view preparation when effective port labels are shown. Endpoint existence, one-wire-per-input, and Sum port-count rules remain owned by their existing operations.
- Add an authored signal-width mode for Gain and Unit Delay, following the existing sample-time mode/field pattern. Empty mode in stored schema-v1 parameters means explicit, and zero width still means explicit scalar width one; this preserves every existing saved block. Newly added Gain and Unit Delay default to inherited width with an unconnected/readout fallback of one. Persist authored mode; an effective width in a resolved copy is display/realization data and must never be rewritten as explicit author intent.
- Explicit widths remain authoritative. An inherited block with an upstream width and non-scalar Unit Delay initial condition of another length fails with the block name and both widths. Widths outside 1..16 fail at the inherited block. A fixed downstream port does not back-propagate; a mismatch uses the existing endpoint/port/channel-count vocabulary. Unresolved unconnected inherited blocks display width one, then retain the existing not-connected compile refusal.
- Preserve Process Lab named-MIMO policy: Matrix Gain, Vector Sum, Vector Constant, Vector Scope, Mux/Demux, Selector/Permutation, State-Space, MIMO Transfer Function, ZPK, FRD, and PID2 retain authored widths and channel names. Width inference never invents or propagates channel names.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Add a persistent public regression in `internal/studio/simulink_vector_routing_fixture_test.go` that currently fails at Connect: Vector Constant `[1,2,3]` -> default inherited Gain `K=2` -> default inherited Unit Delay with scalar initial condition `9` -> three-channel Vector Scope, with no `signal_width` update on Gain or Unit Delay. Connect succeeds, snapshot ports report width three, the first delayed sample is `[9,9,9]`, later samples are `[2,4,6]`, and a second inherited block in the chain proves transitive propagation.
- Gain realization becomes `K*I(width)` only for its resolved 1-D width; scalar behavior and Matrix Gain remain unchanged. Unit Delay uses the same resolved width for ports, state realization, and initial-condition validation.
- New Gain and Unit Delay editor/schema fields expose `signal_width_mode` (`inherited` or `explicit`) plus explicit width using the existing parameter activation metadata. Switching to explicit width restores current validation and refusal behavior.
- `Connect`, connected block edits, full document apply/dry-run, snapshot rendering, and compilation resolve the same effective widths. A conflicting edit/document is rejected atomically and names the implicated block/ports and channel counts; no wire or parameter update is partially persisted.
- Schema-v1 Gain and Unit Delay JSON without a width mode decode as explicit scalar width one and round-trip without behavior change. Dump/apply of an inherited model preserves inherited intent and remains a no-op; inferred width is not converted to explicit state.
- Existing direct Sum semantics remain exact: explicit equal-width multi-input elementwise sum and explicit one-input all-elements reduction. Existing named-MIMO routing and same-width channel rename/fanout tests remain unchanged.
- Update `internal/studio/testdata/simulink/r2026a/sum_and_direct_vectors.json`, `docs/simulink-r2026a-compatibility.md`, and README capability text with the accessed official references and the bounded inherited-width contract.

## Non-goals
- No Sum width inheritance, mixed scalar/vector Sum input expansion, spacer characters, or specified-dimension reduction. Sum has per-input expansion and reduction policy rather than shape preservation; plan it as its own slice.
- No backward propagation, cyclic unknown-width solving, matrices/rank/orientation, N-D or variable-size signals, dynamic resizing during a run, automatic channel-name propagation, bus signals, data types, or new routing blocks.
- No changes to explicitly named MIMO block parameters or to the 16-channel simulation/direct-vector limit.

## Likely Files
- Authority and domain data: `internal/studio/model.go`, new focused `internal/studio/signal_dimensions.go` (or cohesive placement beside `ports.go`), `internal/studio/direct_vector_compatibility.go`, `internal/studio/catalog.go`, `internal/studio/ports.go`.
- Callers/persistence: `internal/studio/studio.go`, `internal/studio/document.go`, `internal/studio/simulate.go`, `internal/studio/store.go`; reuse one graph-loading helper rather than duplicating queries.
- Regressions/docs: `internal/studio/simulink_vector_routing_fixture_test.go`, `internal/studio/port_schema_test.go`, `internal/studio/document_test.go`, `internal/studio/ports_test.go`, `internal/web/server_test.go`, fixture JSON, compatibility doc, README.

## Validation Gates
- Run: `go test ./internal/studio -run 'Test(R2026a.*Vector|Inherited.*SignalWidth|Connect.*Width|VectorFanout|FlowDocument|ApplyFlow|NamedMIMO)' -count=1`.
- Run: `go test ./internal/web -run 'TestWorkbench.*(PortWidth|SignalWidth)' -count=1`.
- Run: `go test ./internal/studio -run 'Test(ScalarPortsKeepWidthOneAndExistingPortIDs|LegacyDirectVectorParametersRemainScalar|AuthoredDirectVectorParametersRoundTrip|NamedMIMOFeedbackCompilesAndSimulatesByPortSchema)' -count=1`.

data.body:
# Let discrete PID controllers inherit model sample time

## Goal
- Let PID and PID2 authors select an inherited discrete sample time so controllers follow one model rate instead of duplicating a numeric setting.
- Preserve the existing LTI realization and make the feature work through the editor, persistence, full-model compilation and simulation, fidelity, frequency analysis, and PID design/apply workflow.

## Context
- Implement after `3AFLOM`. Its `resolveModelSampleTimes(blocks, connections, baseStep)` operation is the sole authority for effective compiled rates. Do not add a PID-specific graph walk, caller-managed propagation order, or a second effective-rate cache.
- The catalog time-domain fields and validation own authored intent only: continuous versus discrete, and explicit versus inherited. Compiled copies may carry the resolved explicit `SampleTime`; saved blocks and provenance must retain `SampleTimeMode=inherited`.
- Current `representationTimeFields` exposes only a numeric discrete sample time and `validateRepresentationTime` requires it to be positive. PID and PID2 already realize through `controlsys` using `representationSampleTime`, so the resolved compilation copy can remain the only input to the realization.
- MathWorks PID Controller documentation, accessed 2026-08-30: https://www.mathworks.com/help/simulink/slref/pidcontroller.html. It defines discrete sample time `-1` as inherited from upstream blocks, while recommending an explicit value when upstream rates may change.
- Candidate ranking from spike `OCEV5Z`:
  1. Inherited discrete rate: medium-high value, depends on `3AFLOM`, low-to-medium risk; it removes duplicated rate configuration and uses the existing linear driver.
  2. Ideal form: medium value, no nonlinear dependency, medium risk; Process Lab must consistently map Ideal P/I/D semantics across PID, PID2, tuning candidates, and the `P=0` edge.
  3. Output saturation: high value, but high dependency and risk; the step partition is metadata only and the production response driver does not execute nonlinear segments or feedback cycles.
  4. Anti-windup: very high value after saturation, but very high dependency and risk; back-calculation or clamping must own integrator state and cannot be a clipped LTI output.
  5. Unfiltered derivative: low-to-medium value and medium risk; it is discrete-only, requires differentiator state and a realization outside current `controlsys` filtered-PID support.
  6. Reset: medium value and high risk; it adds an event input plus integrator/filter state reset semantics.
  7. Tracking: high industrial value and high risk; it adds a tracking port and state feedback for bumpless transfer.
  8. External parameter ports: medium-high gain-scheduling value and very high risk; time-varying P/I/D/N changes are not an LTI system and require dynamic ports and nonlinear execution.
- MathWorks documents output saturation, back-calculation and clamping anti-windup, reset, tracking, and external parameter ports on the same PID page. The official anti-windup example is https://www.mathworks.com/help/simulink/slref/anti-windup-control-using-a-pid-controller.html.
- `controlsys v1.3.0` supports parallel and standard PID conversion but no saturation, anti-windup, reset, tracking, external gains, or unfiltered derivative realization. Process Lab has a `blockDefinition.step` seam and tested execution partition, but no registered step block and no response driver that executes the partition.

## Compatibility and defaults
- Keep new PID and PID2 blocks continuous by default. Keep their stored discrete fallback at `0.1 s` and `SampleTimeMode=explicit`; selecting discrete must not silently change existing or newly authored behavior.
- Saved PID/PID2 parameters with an absent `sampleTimeMode` continue to normalize as explicit. Do not add a schema migration or rewrite stored JSON.
- When inherited is selected, retain the authored numeric `SampleTime` as an inactive fallback value so toggling back to explicit is lossless. Never persist the resolved rate into that field.
- An unanchored inherited PID falls back to the public run or analysis base step under the `3AFLOM` contract. If neither an anchor nor positive base step exists, return the existing actionable inherited-rate error.
- In controller-role extraction, use the already compiled discrete plant `Dt` as inherited controller context when `ControlModelBuildRequest.BaseStep` is omitted. An explicit request base step remains caller policy; a conflict with plant `Dt` must fail through the existing domain validation. Do not inspect raw plant parameters or duplicate sample-time propagation in controller design.

## Acceptance Criteria
- PID and PID2 editor/schema expose `sample_time_mode` only when `time_domain=discrete`; expose numeric `sample_time` only when the domain is discrete and mode is explicit. Published `activeWhen` metadata and server-side active-field validation agree.

- A public full-model compile resolves inherited PID and PID2 rates through the neutral, bidirectional single-rate component behavior delivered by `3AFLOM`. Equal explicit anchors succeed; conflicting anchors fail rather than choosing a rate.

- Update `internal/studio/testdata/simulink/r2026a/pid_parallel_form.json` and `docs/simulink-r2026a-compatibility.md` to describe the supported inherited-rate subset and analytic provenance without claiming MATLAB-produced output.

## Non-goals
- Ideal form; unfiltered derivative; alternate discrete integrator/filter methods; initial-condition ports; reset; output or integrator saturation; anti-windup; tracking; external P/I/D/N or saturation-limit ports.
- A general nonlinear or hybrid segment driver, step-block feedback-cycle support, multirate segmented zero-order-hold execution, triggered or conditionally executed subsystems, variable sample time, or changing PID/PID2 defaults.

- `internal/studio/control_models.go` and `internal/studio/pid_design.go`: bridge compiled plant `Dt` into an extracted inherited controller and preserve authored mode during apply.
